[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/86/Thirteenth_chord_CMA13%28sharp11%29.mid/Thirteenth_chord_CMA13%28sharp11%29.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thirteenth_chord_CMA13(sharp11).mid "File:Thirteenth chord CMA13(sharp11).mid")[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Russell%27s_six_lydian_scales.png/250px-Russell%27s_six_lydian_scales.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Russell's_six_lydian_scales.png) Russell's original six Lydian scales[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-1) The _**Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization**_ is a 1953 jazz music theory book written by [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). The book is the founding text of the Lydian Chromatic Concept (LCC), or Lydian Chromatic Theory (LCT). Russell's work postulates that all music is based on the tonal gravity of the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode"). ## Deriving Lydian \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Deriving Lydian")\] Russell believed that [dominant function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominant_function "Dominant function") is the driving force behind all harmonic motion. Russell focuses on the Lydian mode because it can be built with fifths. For instance, to construct a C Lydian scale one could list the first seven tones on the [circle of fifths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_of_fifths "Circle of fifths") starting with C, the desired Lydian Tonic. This process would yield C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯. If these tones are voiced in the space of an octave, they form the Lydian mode; specifically, C Lydian (C, D, E, F♯, G, A, B).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Deriving_Lydian_with_Fifths-2) Additionally, Russell observed, when these tones are voiced in thirds they form the preferred form of a major 13 (#11) chord.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-13th_chord_derivation-3) ## The Lydian Chromatic Scale \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: The Lydian Chromatic Scale")\] Russell builds a prototype chromatic scale starting on the Lydian Tonic by stacking fifths, skipping the interval between the seventh and eighth tones, and placing the skipped tone at the end for having the lowest level of tonal gravity. Using C as the Lydian Tonic yields the following 12-note scale with [enharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enharmonic "Enharmonic") respellings: C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯, G♯, E♭ (D♯), B♭ (A♯), F (E♯), D♭ (C♯). Thus the Lydian Chromatic Scale and all its derivatives contain only [Pythagorean intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_interval "Pythagorean interval").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-4) ## Tonal gravity \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tonal gravity")\] Russell posited that tonal gravity emanates from the first seven tones of the Lydian mode. As the player ventures further from the Lydian tonic however (and further up the circle of fifths), the tonal gravity shifts. For example, if notes further up the circle of fifths (e.g. ♯2/♭3) are used, the tonal gravity is probably shifting.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Tonal_gravity-5) ## Influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Influence")\] Russell's theory has had far-reaching effect especially in the realm of modal jazz. [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer") said that it "opens the door to countless means of melodic expression"[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-6) and critic [Joachim-Ernst Berendt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim-Ernst_Berendt "Joachim-Ernst Berendt") described it as "the first work deriving a theory of jazz harmony from the immanent laws of jazz" and as "the pathbreaker for [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s 'modality'".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-7) [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans") and Miles Davis used the theory[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Russell's_relationship_with_Evans-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Impact_of_LCC-9) to record modal jazz such as the album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_. John Coltrane's modal jazz is usually analyzed using Russell's method.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Modal_Trane-10) In arguably his most famous piece, " [Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps_(composition) "Giant Steps (composition)")," Coltrane can be heard traveling through a succession of three parent Lydian Chromatic scales: C Lydian, A♭ Lydian, and E Lydian.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-11) Additionally, many conservatories teach Russell's theory to varying degrees.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Impact_of_LCC2-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Teaching_LCC-13) ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: See also")\] - [Chord-scale system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord-scale_system "Chord-scale system") ## Notes \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Notes")\] 01. - gamelan | Musical artist **Donald Eugene Cherry** (November 18, 1936 – October 19, 1995)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-1) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist. Beginning in the late 1950s, he had a long tenure performing in the bands of saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), including on the pioneering [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ (1959) and _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ (1961). Cherry also collaborated separately with musicians including [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five"), and [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). Cherry released his debut album as bandleader, _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_, in 1966. In the 1970s, he became a pioneer in [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), with his work drawing on African, Middle Eastern, and [Hindustani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") music, as heard on the 1975 release _[Brown Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Rice_(album) "Brown Rice (album)")_. He was a member of the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), along with percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and sitar and tabla player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-2) Chris Kelsey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called Cherry "one of the most influential jazz musicians of the late 20th century."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-3) ## Early life Cherry was born in [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), to a mother of [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") descent and an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") father.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-4) His mother and grandmother played piano and his father played trumpet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) His father owned Oklahoma City's Cherry Blossom Club, which hosted performances by jazz musicians [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") and [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6) In 1940, Cherry moved with his family to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where his father tended bar at the Plantation Club on [Central Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Avenue_(Los_Angeles) "Central Avenue (Los Angeles)"), at the time the center of a vibrant jazz scene.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-carr-8) Cherry recalled skipping school at [Fremont High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fremont_High_School "John C. Fremont High School") in order to play with the [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") band at [Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) This resulted in his transfer to Jacob Riis High School, a [reform school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_school "Reform school"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) where he met drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-crouch-10) ## Career By the early 1950s Cherry was playing with jazz musicians in Los Angeles, sometimes acting as pianist in [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer")'s group.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 While trumpeter [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown") was in Los Angeles with [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), Cherry attended a jam session with Brown and [Larance Marable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larance_Marable "Larance Marable") at [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy")'s house, and Brown informally mentored Cherry.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) He also toured with saxophonist [James Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clay_(musician) "James Clay (musician)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):45 Cherry became well known in 1958 when he performed and recorded with [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), first in a quintet with pianist [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley") and later in the quartet which recorded for [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). During this period, "his lines ... gathered much of their freedom of motion from the free harmonic structures."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):289 Cherry co-led _[The Avant-Garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avant-Garde_(album) "The Avant-Garde (album)")_ session which saw [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") replacing Coleman in the quartet, recorded and toured with [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins"), was a member of the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five") with [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai"), and recorded and toured with both [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") and [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). His first recording as a leader was _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_ for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1965. The band included Coleman's drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell") as well as saxophonist [Gato Barbieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gato_Barbieri "Gato Barbieri"), whom he had met while touring Europe with Ayler, and bassist [Henry Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Grimes "Henry Grimes").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-13) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg/500px-Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg) Cherry at Park Le Cascine, [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy, September 1975 After leaving Coleman's quartet, Cherry often played in small groups and duets, many with ex-Coleman drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), during a long sojourn in [Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") and other locations. He traveled through Europe, India, Morocco, South Africa, and elsewhere to explore and play with a variety of musicians. In the late 1960s he settled in [Tågarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A5garp "Tågarp"), Sweden with his wife, Swedish designer and textile artist Moki Cherry. In 1968, Don Cherry taught music classes with guest lecturers, performance collaborators, and workshop leaders from around the world at Arbetarnas bildningsförbund (ABF) House, a Swedish labor movement-run education center. For ten years, Don and Moki Cherry lived and worked collaboratively in an abandoned schoolhouse in Tågarp, holding classes and performances, hosting guests and collaborators, and exploring their concept of Organic Music Society. In 1969, Cherry played trumpet and other instruments for poet [Allen Ginsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Ginsberg "Allen Ginsberg")'s 1970 LP _[Songs of Innocence and Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_Experience_(Allen_Ginsberg_album) "Songs of Innocence and Experience (Allen Ginsberg album)")_, a musical adaptation of [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake")'s [poetry collection of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_of_Experience "Songs of Innocence and of Experience").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-Jurek-14) He appeared on Coleman's 1971 LP _[Science Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Fiction_(Ornette_Coleman_album) "Science Fiction (Ornette Coleman album)")_, and from 1976 to 1987 reunited with Blackwell and fellow Coleman alumni [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") and [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden") as [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-15) Old and New Dreams recorded four albums (two for [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") and two for [Black Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note "Black Saint/Soul Note")) where Cherry's "subtlety of rhythmic expansion and contraction" was noted.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):290 [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Don_Cherry_1989.jpg/500px-Don_Cherry_1989.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Cherry_1989.jpg) Don Cherry in 1989 In the 1970s, Cherry ventured into the developing genre of world fusion music. Cherry incorporated influences of Middle Eastern, African, and Indian music into his playing. He studied Indian music with [Vasant Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasant_Rai "Vasant Rai") in the early seventies. From 1978 to 1982, he recorded three albums for ECM with "world jazz" group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), consisting of Cherry, percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar") and [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9) Cherry also collaborated with classical composer [Krzysztof Penderecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Penderecki "Krzysztof Penderecki") on the 1971 album _[Actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actions_(album) "Actions (album)")_. In 1973, he co-composed the score for [Alejandro Jodorowsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Jodorowsky "Alejandro Jodorowsky")'s film _[The Holy Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holy_Mountain_(1973_film) "The Holy Mountain (1973 film)")_, together with Jodorowsky and Ronald Frangipane. At the end of the 1970s, the trio Organic Music Theater (with Gian Piero Pramaggiore and [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos")) had an intense live activity in Italy and France. In 1982, Cherry released the duet album _[El Corazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Coraz%C3%B3n_(Don_Cherry_and_Ed_Blackwell_album) "El Corazón (Don Cherry and Ed Blackwell album)")_ with Ed Blackwell. He also released two albums as a bandleader in the 1980s: _[Home Boy (Sister Out)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Boy_(Sister_Out) "Home Boy (Sister Out)")_ in 1985 and _[Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco_(album) "Art Deco (album)")_ in 1988. He recorded again with the original Ornette Coleman Quartet on the first disc of Coleman's 1987 album _[In All Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_All_Languages "In All Languages")_. Other playing opportunities in his career came with [Carla Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Bley "Carla Bley")'s 1971 opera _[Escalator over the Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator_over_the_Hill "Escalator over the Hill")_ and as a sideman on recordings by [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed"), [Ian Dury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Dury "Ian Dury"), [Rip Rig + Panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rip_Rig_+_Panic "Rip Rig + Panic"), and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"). Cherry played with Ian Dury and the Blockheads on their 1980 tour, including the final gig on Christmas Eve, which was broadcast live by the BBC, from the [Dominion Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Theatre "Dominion Theatre") in London, on _[The Old Grey Whistle Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Old_Grey_Whistle_Test "The Old Grey Whistle Test")_. He also toured UK and Europe with the band in 1981.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-16) In 1992, Don Cherry was invited by renowned Indian violinist [L. Shankar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Shankar "L. Shankar") to perform in Mumbai, India. This interaction was captured in a documentary film titled "Rhythms of the World: Bombay and all the Jazz". In 1994, Cherry appeared on the [Red Hot Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Organization "Red Hot Organization")'s compilation _[Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolen_Moments:_Red_Hot_+_Cool "Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool")_, on a track titled "Apprehension", alongside [the Watts Prophets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Watts_Prophets "The Watts Prophets").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-17) This album, meant to raise awareness of the [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") epidemic among African-Americans, was named "Album of the Year" by _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_. ## Death and legacy Cherry died of liver cancer in [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), Spain, on October 19, 1995, at the age of 58.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) Cherry was inducted into the [Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Jazz_Hall_of_Fame "Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame") in 2011.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-18) ## Family and personal life Cherry was married to Monika Karlsson ( [Moki Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moki_Cherry "Moki Cherry")), a Swedish painter and textile artist, who also occasionally played [tanpura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanpura "Tanpura") with him.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) His stepdaughter [Neneh Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neneh_Cherry "Neneh Cherry"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) his step-granddaughters [Mabel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabel_(singer) "Mabel (singer)") and Tyson, and his sons David Ornette Cherry, Christian Cherry, and [Eagle-Eye Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle-Eye_Cherry "Eagle-Eye Cherry"), are also musicians. David Ornette Cherry died from an asthma attack at the age of 64 on November 20, 2022.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-20) Don Cherry practiced [Vajrayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vajrayana "Vajrayana") Buddhism.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-22) ## Instruments Cherry learned to play various brass instruments in high school.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 Throughout his career, he played an F. [Besson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besson_(music_company) "Besson (music company)") (Paris) MEHA pocket cornet[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-23) (though he identified this as a [pocket trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_trumpet "Pocket trumpet")), trumpet, [cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet "Cornet"), [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), and [bugle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugle "Bugle").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-pocketcornets-25) Cherry began his career as a pianist, and continued playing piano and organ as secondary instruments throughout his career.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) After returning from a musical and cultural journey through Africa, he often played the _donso ngoni_, a harp-lute with a gourd body originating from West Africa (see _[ngoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoni_(instrument) "Ngoni (instrument)")_). During his international journeys, Cherry also collected a variety of non-Western instruments, which he mastered and often played in performances and on recordings. Among these instruments were [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [bamboo flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo_flute "Bamboo flute") and assorted percussion instruments.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) ## Technique and style Cherry's trumpet influences included [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), and [Harry Edison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweets_Edison "Sweets Edison").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Journalist Howard Mandel suggests [Henry "Red" Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Allen "Red Allen") as a precedent (given Allen's "blustery rather than Armstrong-brazen brass sound, jauntily unpredictable melodic streams, squeezed-off and/or half-valve effects and repertoire including novelty vocals")[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) while Ekkehard Jost cites [Wild Bill Davison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Davison "Bill Davison").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):138 Some critics have noted shortcomings in Cherry's technique.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) [Ron Wynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wynn "Ron Wynn") writes that "\[Cherry's\] technique isn't always the most efficient; frequently, his rapid-fired solos contain numerous missed or muffed notes. But he's a master at exploring the trumpet and cornet's expressive, voice-like properties; he bends notes and adds slurs and smears, and his twisting solos are tightly constructed and executed regardless of their flaws."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Jost notes the tendency for writers to focus on Cherry's "technical insecurity", but asserts that "the problem lies elsewhere. Perfect technical control in extremely fast tempos was more or less risk-free as long as the improviser had to deal with standard changes that were familiar to him from years of working with them.... In the music of the Ornette Coleman Quartet—a 'new-found-land' where the laws and habits of functional harmony do not apply—there is no use for patterns that had been worked out on that basis."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137 Miles Davis was initially dismissive of Cherry's playing, claiming that "anyone can tell that guy's not a trumpet player—it's just notes that come out, and every note he plays he looks serious about, and people will go for that, especially white people."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) According to Cherry, however, when Davis attended an Ornette Coleman performance at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"), he was impressed with Cherry's playing and sat in with the group using Cherry's pocket trumpet.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) Later, in a 1964 _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ blindfold test, Davis indicated that he liked Cherry's # Codona Codona Free jazz and world fusion ensemble | Codona | | --- | | Genres | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")
[World fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_fusion "World fusion") | | Years active | 1978(1978)–1982(1982) | | Labels | [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") | | | | Past members | [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)")
[Nana Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Vasconcelos "Nana Vasconcelos")
[Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott") | **Codona** was a [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_fusion "World fusion") group which released three self-titled albums on the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") label in 1979, 1981 and 1983. The trio consisted of [multi-instrumentalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-instrumentalist "Multi-instrumentalist") [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)"), [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott"), and [Nana Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Vasconcelos "Nana Vasconcelos"). The name of the group was derived from the first two letters of the musicians' first names (COllin, DOn, NAna).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-1) The members of the group declared that their goal was "to be open and incorporate all we know, without turning the whole world into milk toast - still encouraging the survival of the traditions".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-2) Critic [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(American_writer) "Robert Palmer (American writer)") stated that the group's "self-appointed mission is to fuse African, Indian and other music traditions in the heat of improvisation".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-3) The authors of [The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz") on CD called the group's debut album "one of the iconic episodes in so-called (but never better called) 'world music'", and stated: "Any tendency to regard Codona's music... as floating impressionism is sheer prejudice, for all these performances are deeply rooted in modern jazz (Coltrane's harmonies and rhythms, Ornette Coleman's melodic and rhythmic primitivism) and in another great and related improvisational tradition from Brazil."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-4) ## Background The musicians had crossed paths on a number of occasions prior to the formation of the group in 1977.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-5) Vasconcelos appeared on Cherry's album _[Organic Music Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_Music_Society "Organic Music Society")_, recorded and released in 1972,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-6) while Walcott played on Cherry's _[Hear & Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hear_&_Now_(Don_Cherry_album) "Hear & Now (Don Cherry album)")_, recorded in 1976 and released in 1977.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-7) Cherry also appeared on Walcott's _[Grazing Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing_Dreams "Grazing Dreams")_, recorded and released in 1977,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-8) while both Walcott and Vasconcelos played on [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti")'s _[Sol do Meio Dia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_do_Meio_Dia "Sol do Meio Dia")_, recorded in 1977 and released in 1978.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-9) The members' involvement with Codona overlapped with their participation in other projects, Cherry with [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams"), Walcott with [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_(band) "Oregon (band)"), and Vasconcelos with [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), [Milton Nascimento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento"), [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell"), and others. Although the group was conceived as a leaderless trio, Walcott was the organizer and primary composer.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-11) Codona was noted for its use of a broad range of instrumentation.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) While Cherry was primarily known as a trumpet and cornet player, he also performed on various [flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"), [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_(music) "Organ (music)"), [melodica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodica "Melodica"), and the [Malian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali") doussn’gouni.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) Walcott played [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar"), [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla"), [hammered dulcimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammered_dulcimer "Hammered dulcimer"), [sanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbira "Mbira"), and [timpani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timpani "Timpani"), while Vasconcelos performed on [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [cuica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuica "Cuica"), [talking drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_drum "Talking drum"), and a variety of [percussion instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) In addition, all three musicians sang.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) The group was also known for its unusual arrangements, an example being "Colemanwonder", a medley of two [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") tunes combined with [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder")'s " [Sir Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Duke "Sir Duke")", performed on trumpet, sitar, cuica, and percussion, and appearing on the group's [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona_(album) "Codona (album)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) The group disbanded following Walcott's death in a traffic accident in [East Released: 1974 | | | _**Head Hunters**_ is the twelfth [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by American pianist, keyboardist and composer [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released October 26, 1973, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Recording sessions for the album took place in the evening at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") and [Different Fur Trading Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_Fur "Different Fur") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Hancock is featured with woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") from his previous "Mwandishi" sextet and three new collaborators – bassist [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)"), percussionist [Bill Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Summers_(musician) "Bill Summers (musician)"), and drummer [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason"). The latter group of collaborators, which would go on to be known as [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), also played on Hancock's subsequent studio album _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974). All of the musicians (with the exception of Mason) play multiple instruments on the album. The album was a commercial and artistic breakthrough for Hancock, crossing over to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences and bringing [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") to mainstream attention, peaking at number 13 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Today the album is regarded as a landmark of fusion and has influenced artists in numerous other genres. In 2008, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") inducted it into the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically important".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-3) ## Background and recording _Head Hunters_ followed three experimental albums by Hancock's "Mwandishi" sextet: _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_, _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, and _[Sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_(album) "Sextant (album)")_, released between 1971 and 1973. He later reflected on moving away from this style: > I began to feel that I had been spending so much time exploring the upper atmosphere of music and the more ethereal kind of far-out spacey stuff. Now there was this need to take some more of the earth and to feel a little more tethered; a connection to the earth. ... I was beginning to feel that we (the sextet) were playing this heavy kind of music, and I was tired of everything being heavy. I wanted to play something lighter. —Hancock's sleeve notes: 1997 CD reissue For the new album, Hancock assembled a new band, [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), of whom only woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") had been a member of the "Mwandishi" sextet. Hancock handled all synthesizer parts himself, having shared these duties with [Patrick Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gleeson "Patrick Gleeson") on _Crossings_ and _Sextant,_ and decided against the use of guitar altogether in favor of the Hohner [Clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet"), one of the defining sounds on the album. The new band featured a tight [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") composed of [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)") (bass guitar) and [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason") (drums), creating a relaxed [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") sensibility that gave it an appeal to a wider audience. Of the four tracks on the album, " [Watermelon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_Man_(composition) "Watermelon Man (composition)")" was the only one not written for the album. A hit from Hancock's [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") days, originally appearing on his debut _[Takin' Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takin'_Off "Takin' Off")_ (1962) and later covered by [Mongo Santamaría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría"), it was reworked by Hancock and Mason for this album, featuring Bill Summers blowing into a beer bottle in imitation of the [hindewho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_music "Pygmy music") flute used by the Mbuti [Pygmies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_peoples "Pygmy peoples") of [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"). The track features heavy use of African percussion. "Sly" was dedicated to [Sly Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_Stone "Sly Stone") of [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone"). "Chameleon" features a famous bassline played by Hancock on an [ARP Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_Odyssey "ARP Odyssey") synthesizer. Closing track "Vein Melter" is a slow-burner, predominantly featuring Hancock on [Rhodes piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_piano "Rhodes piano") and Maupin on [bass clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet"). Heavily edited versions of "Chameleon" and "Vein Melter" were released as two sides of a 45 RPM single. The Headhunters band, with [Mike Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Clark_(drummer) "Mike Clark (drummer)") replacing Mason, worked with Hancock on a number of other albums, including _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974), _[Man-Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-Child "Man-Child")_ (1975), and _[Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Flood (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1975). The subsequent albums _[_Secrets_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secrets_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Secrets (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1976) and _[Sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight_(jazz_album) "Sunlight (jazz album)")_ (1977), had widely diverging personnel. The Headhunters, with Hancock featured as a guest soloist, produced the albums _[Survival of the Fittest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_Fittest_(album) "Survival of the Fittest (album)")_ (1975) and _Straight from the Gate_ (1978), the first of which was produced by Hancock and included the hit "God Make Me Funky". ## Album cover The album cover, designed by [Victor Moscoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso "Victor Moscoso"), features Hancock wearing a mask based on the _[kple kple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goli_(dance) "Goli (dance)")_ mask of the [Baoulé people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baoul%C3%A9_people "Baoulé people") of [Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast"). Positioned clockwise around Hancock from lower left are Mason, Jackson, Maupin, and Summers. ## Release and reception The album was released on October 26th, 1973. The album was remixed for [quadraphonic sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadraphonic_sound "Quadraphonic sound") in 1974. Columbia released this mix on [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") in the [Stereo Quadraphonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Quadraphonic "Stereo Quadraphonic") matrix format and [8-track tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8-track_cartridge "8-track cartridge"). The quadraphonic mixes feature elements not heard in the stereo version, including an additional keyboard melody at the beginning of "Sly". Surround sound versions of the album have been released a number of times on the [Super Audio CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Audio_CD "Super Audio CD") format, using a digital transfer of the original four-channel quad mix re-purposed into [5.1 surround sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.1_surround_sound "5.1 surround sound"). ### Commercial performance _Head Hunters_ was a commercial success, peaking at No. 13 on the [Billboard 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and at No. 2 on the [Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_R&B/Hip-Hop_Albums "Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums") chart. The album remained in the top 30 and top 5 respectively for each chart into the end of the next year. Ultimately, _Head Hunters_ became the biggest-selling jazz album of all time until surpassed by [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson")'s _[Breezin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breezin' "Breezin'")_ in 1976.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ## Reception and | Professional ratings The album received contemporary critical acclaim and continues to receive acclaim. Writing for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Stephen Thomas Erlewine would say, "Head Hunters was a pivotal point in Herbie Hancock's career, bringing him into the vanguard of jazz fusion. Hancock had pushed avant-garde boundaries on his own albums and with Miles Davis, but he had never devoted himself to the groove as he did on Head Hunters," concluding, "Jazz purists, of course, decried the experiments at the time, but Head Hunters still sounds fresh and vital decades after its initial release, and its genre-bending proved vastly influential on not only jazz, but funk, soul, and hip-hop." Writing for [Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)"), Jeremy Larson would say, "Head Hunters is the bond that connects unnamable forces at the center of jazz and of funk, divine aspirations and base desires, head and body. It’s foolish to try to name the spark of music like this, a parlor game better left to the comedown of an acid trip or a street preacher on his last leg. Head Hunters isn’t the god, it’s just five consummate pros jamming, with a light amount of editing and production." In 2005, the album was ranked number 498 in the book version of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine's list of [the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time"). While it was not included in _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")'_ s original 2003 online version of the list, nor its 2012 revision, it was ranked at number 254 in the 2020 revision.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-11) _Head Hunters_ was a key release in Hancock's career and a defining moment in the genre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and has been an inspiration not only for jazz musicians, but also to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), [jazz funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funk "Jazz funk") and [hip hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") artists.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-Erlewine-2) The [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") added it to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry"), which collects "culturally, historically or aesthetically important" sound recordings from the 20th century.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-12) It was included in the book [1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die"). ## | Professional ratings _**Mwandishi**_ is the ninth studio album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released in March 1971. It is the first album to officially feature Hancock’s ‘Mwandishi’ sextet, consisting of reed player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), trumpeter [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"), trombonist [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams"), and drummer [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"). ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] This album is one of Hancock's first departures from the traditional idioms of jazz, as well as the beginning of an original and creative style which eventually appealed to a wider audience. In addition, _Mwandishi_ was Hancock's attempt at continuing the musical principles and styles he explored in his previous experiences with [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") (on the album _[In A Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_A_Silent_Way "In A Silent Way")_, for instance). Hancock's previous explorations of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") included _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_, an album related to the TV special ‘’ [Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Hey,_Hey,_It's_Fat_Albert "Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert")’’. _Mwandishi_ was recorded at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") Studio C, San Francisco, in January 1971. The recording incorporated progressive notions of funk, jazz, and rock. The tracks on _Mwandishi_ include "Ostinato," the [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature") of which is **15** **8**, "You'll Know When You Get There," and "Wandering Spirit Song." "Wandering Spirit Song" features Hancock's extensive use of tension and release, in which he builds the tension of the song by crescendos and an increasing number of musical voices, and then releases the tension with long held chords on his [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"). _[Mwandishi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mwandishi#Swahili "wikt:mwandishi")_ ("composer") is the [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili "Swahili") name Hancock adopted during the late 1960s and early 1970s. The members of the Sextet each adopted a Swahili name: _[Mchezaji](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mchezaji#Swahili "wikt:mchezaji")_ ("player," someone who plays a game) for [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams"), _[Jabali](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/jabali#Swahili "wikt:jabali")_ ("strong as a rock") for [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"), _[Mganga](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mganga#Swahili "wikt:mganga")_ ("doctor," whose traditional functions include exorcism, prophecy, and the removal of spells) for [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"), Mwile ("body", from Swahili _[mwili](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mwili#Swahili "wikt:mwili")_) for [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), _[Pepo](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pepo#Swahili "wikt:pepo")_ _[Mtoto](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mtoto#Swahili "wikt:mtoto")_ ("demon baby") for [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester"), and _[Ndugu](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/ndugu#Swahili "wikt:ndugu")_ ("brother") for [Leon Chancler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_%22Ndugu%22_Chancler "Leon \"Ndugu\" Chancler"). ## Release history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Release history")\] _Mwandishi_, along with _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_ and _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, was reissued in one set as _Mwandishi: The Complete Warner Bros. - [space rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rock "Space rock") | **Progressive rock** (shortened to **prog rock** or simply **prog**) is a broad [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199871%E2%80%9375-9) that primarily developed in the United States and United Kingdom through the mid- to late 1960s. Initially termed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")", the style emerged from [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") bands who abandoned standard [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") or [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") traditions in favour of [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumentation_(music) "Instrumentation (music)") and [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_(music) "Composition (music)") techniques more commonly associated with [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), while retaining the instrumentation typical of rock music. Additional elements contributed to its " [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")" label: lyrics were more poetic, technology was harnessed for new sounds, music approached the condition of " [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music")", and the studio, rather than the stage, [became the focus of musical activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument"), which often involved creating music for listening rather than dancing. Progressive rock includes a fusion of styles, approaches and genres, and tends to be diverse and [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music"). Progressive rock is often associated with long solos, extended pieces, fantastic lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill and [virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso"). While the genre is often cited for its merging of [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") and [low culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_culture "Low culture"), few artists incorporated Western classical themes in their work to a significant degree, with only a minority of groups ( [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), [Ekseption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekseption "Ekseption"), etc.) directly emulating or referencing classical music. In the early to mid-1970s, progressive rock groups such as [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") and [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") experienced great worldwide success; in the late 1970s, it declined in popularity, and has never fully recovered.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) [Conventional wisdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_wisdom "Conventional wisdom") holds that the rise of [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") caused this, but several more factors contributed to the decline.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) Music critics, who often labelled the style of progressive rock as "pretentious" and the sounds as "pompous" and "overblown", tended to be hostile towards the genre or to completely ignore it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucky20007-11) After the late 1970s, progressive rock fragmented into numerous forms. Some bands achieved commercial success well into the 1980s (albeit with changed lineups and more compact song structures) or crossed into [symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop"), [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock"), or [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"). Early groups who exhibited progressive features are retroactively described as " [proto-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-prog "Proto-prog")". The [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene"), originating in the late 1960s, denotes a subset of progressive rock bands who emphasised the use of [wind instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_instrument "Wind instrument"), complex chord changes and long improvisations. [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition"), from the late 1970s, was more [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde"), and when combined with the Canterbury style, created [avant-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-prog "Avant-prog"). In the 1980s, a new subgenre, [neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"), enjoyed some commercial success, although it was also accused of being derivative and lacking in innovation. [Post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive") draws upon newer developments in popular music and the avant-garde since the mid-1970s. ## Definition and characteristics Further information: [Progressive music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music") ### Scope and related terms ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) [The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Fourth_Colour.mp3 "File:The Fourth Colour.mp3") _[The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fourth_Colour "The Fourth Colour")_, a progressive rock song by [King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Gizzard_and_the_Lizard_Wizard "King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard"). * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ See also: [Progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop") and [Art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock") The term "progressive rock" is related to and sometimes considered [synonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym "Synonym") with " [art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock")", "classical rock" (not to be confused with [classic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_rock "Classic rock")), and "symphonic rock".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Historically, "art rock" has been used to describe at least two related, but distinct, types of rock music.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13) The first is progressive rock as it is generally understood, while the second usage refers to [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") groups who rejected [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia") and the [hippie counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") in favour of a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist"), [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") approach.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13)[\[nb 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-16) Similarities between the two terms are that they both describe a mostly British attempt to elevate rock music to new levels of artistic credibility. However, art rock is more likely to have experimental or avant-garde influences.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) "Prog" was devised in the 1990s[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) as a shorthand term, but later became a transferable adjective, also suggesting a wider palette than that drawn on by the most popular 1970s bands.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20119-19) Progressive rock is varied and is based on fusions of styles, approaches, and genres, tapping into broader cultural resonances that connect to avant-garde art, [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") and [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), performance and the moving image.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Although a unidirectional English "progressive" style emerged in the late 1960s, by 1967, progressive rock had come to constitute a diversity of loosely associated style codes.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) When the "progressive" label arrived, the music was dubbed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")" before it was called "progressive rock",[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore200422-22)[\[nb 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-24) with the term "progressive" referring to the wide range of attempts to break with standard pop music formula.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaworthSmith1975126-25) A number of additional factors contributed to the acquired "progressive" label: lyrics were more poetic; technology was harnessed for new sounds; music approached the condition of "art"; some harmonic language was imported from jazz and [19th-century classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_music "Romantic music"); [the album format overtook singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Era "Album Era"); and the studio, rather than the stage, became the focus of musical activity, which often involved creating music for listening, not dancing.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016201%E2%80%93202-26) > One of the best ways to define progressive rock is that it is a heterogeneous and troublesome genre – a formulation that becomes clear the moment we leave behind characterizations based only on the most visible bands of the early to mid-1970s — [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Critics of the genre often limit its scope to a stereotype of long solos, overlong albums, fantasy lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) While progressive rock is often cited for its merging of high culture and low culture, few artists incorporated literal classical themes in their work to any great degree,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316,_85%E2%80%9387-28) and only a handful of groups purposely emulated or referenced classical music.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Writer Emily Robinson says that the narrowed definition of "progressive rock" was a measure against the term's loose application in the late 1960s, when it was "applied to everyone from [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") to [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones")". Debate over the genre's criterion continued to the 2010s, particularly on [Internet forums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_forum "Internet forum") dedicated to prog.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) According to musicologists [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell, [Bill Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Martin_(philosophy) "Bill Martin (philosophy)") and Edward Macan authored major books about progressive rock while "effectively accept\[ing\] the characterization of progressive rock offered by its critics. ... they each do so largely unconsciously."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) Academic John S. Cotner contests Macan's view that progressive rock cannot exist without the continuous and overt assimilation of classical music into rock.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) Author Kevin Holm-Hudson agrees that "progressive rock is a style far more diverse than what is heard from its mainstream groups and what is implied by unsympathetic critics."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316-29) ### Relation to art and social in music") In early references to the music, "progressive" was partly related to [progressive politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_politics "Progressive politics"), but those hence involves a continuous aesthetic movement between [formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formalism_(art) "Formalism (art)") and [eclecticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-32) Cotner also says that progressive rock incorporates both formal and eclectic elements, "It consists of a combination of factors – some We can see rock 'n' roll as a deconstruction and 'progressive' music as a reconstruction."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWillis2014219-35) Author Will Romano states that "rock itself can be interpreted as a progressive idea... Ironically, and quite paradoxically, 'progressive rock', the classic era of the late 1960s through the mid- and late 1970s, introduces not only the explosive and exploratory sounds of technology... but traditional music forms (classical and European folk) and (often) a pastiche compositional style and artificial constructs ( [concept albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album")) which suggests [postmodernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism")."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERomano201024-36) ### Use of synthesizers [Synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") have a long history in the creation of progressive rock, beginning with the perhaps most well known early electronic instrument, the [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin "Theremin"). legion of young bands that were to create progressive rock in the early 1970s".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEverett199995-45) Dylan's poetry, [the Mothers "Freak Out!")_ (1966) and the Beatles' _[Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band")_ (1967) were all important in progressive rock's development.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) The productions of [Phil Spector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Spector "Phil Spector") were key influences,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199847-46) as they introduced the possibility of using the recording studio to create music that otherwise could never be achieved.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm199529-47) Other influences include the Beach Boys' _[Pet Sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sounds "Pet Sounds")_ (1966), which [Brian Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Wilson "Brian Wilson") intended as an answer to _Rubber Soul_[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-48) and which in turn influenced the Beatles when they made _Sgt. Pepper_.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199853-49)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200130-50) Dylan introduced a literary element to rock through his fascination with the [Surrealists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") and the [French Symbolists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolism_(movement) "Symbolism (movement)"), and his immersion in the New York City art scene of the early 1960s.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987156-7-51) The trend of bands with names drawn from literature, such as [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors"), [Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band) "Steppenwolf (band)") and [the Ides of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ides_of_March_(band) "The Ides of March (band)"), were a further sign of rock music aligning itself with high culture.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987179-52) Dylan also led the way in blending rock with folk music styles. This was followed by folk rock groups such as the Byrds, who based their initial sound on that of the Beatles.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-53) In turn, the Byrds' vocal harmonies inspired those of [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)"),[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin19964-54) and [British folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_folk_rock "British folk rock") bands like [Fairport Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairport_Convention "Fairport Convention"), who emphasised instrumental virtuosity.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201154%E2%80%9355-55) Some of these artists, such as [the Incredible String Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incredible_String_Band "The Incredible String Band") and [Shirley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Collins "Shirley Collins") and [Dolly Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Collins "Dolly Collins"), would prove influential through their use of instruments borrowed from world music and [early music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_music "Early music").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers200472,204-56) #### _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_ Main articles: [Pet Sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sounds "Pet Sounds") and [Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band") > Many groups and musicians played important roles in this development process, but none more than [the Beach Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beach_Boys "The Beach Boys") and [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")... \[They\] brought expansions in [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony"), [instrumentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement "Arrangement") (and therefore [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre")), [duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duration_(music) "Duration (music)"), [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"), and the use of [recording technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_multitrack_recording "History of multitrack recording"). Of these elements, the first and last were the most important in clearing a pathway toward the development of progressive rock. —Bill Martin[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839-57) _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_, with their lyrical unity, extended structure, complexity, eclecticism, experimentalism, and influences derived from classical music forms, are largely viewed as beginnings in the progressive rock genre[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199715,20-58)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839%E2%80%9340-59) and as turning points wherein rock, which previously had been considered dance music, became music that was made for listening to.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19973-60)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839-57) Between _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_, the Beach Boys released the single " [Good Vibrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Vibrations "Good Vibrations")" (1966), dubbed a " [pocket symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_symphony "Pocket symphony")" by [Derek Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Taylor "Derek Taylor"), the band's publicist. The song contained an eclectic array of exotic instruments and several disjunctive key and modal shifts.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooneCovach199741%E2%80%9346-61) Scott Interrante of _[Popmatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popmatters "Popmatters")_ wrote that its influence on progressive rock and the psychedelic movement "can't be overstated".[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-62) Martin likened the song to the Beatles' " [A Day in the Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Day_in_the_Life "A Day in the Life")" from _Sgt. Pepper_, in that they showcase "the same reasons why much progressive rock is difficult to dance to".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199840-63) Although _Sgt. Pepper_ was preceded by several albums that had begun to bridge the line between "disposable" pop and "serious" rock, it successfully gave an established "commercial" voice to an alternative youth culture[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson200810-64) and marked the point at which the [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") emerged as a creative format whose importance was equal to or greater than that of the single.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65)[\[nb 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-67) [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford"), a veteran of several progressive rock bands, said that _Sgt. Pepper_ transformed both musicians' ideas of what was possible and audiences' ideas of what was acceptable in music.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012b-68) He believed that: "Without the Beatles, or someone else who had done what the Beatles did, it is fair to assume that there would have been no progressive rock."[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruford2012159-69) In the aftermath of _Sgt. Pepper_, magazines such as [Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker") drew a sharp line between "pop" and "rock". Americans increasingly used the adjective "progressive" for groups like [Jethro Tull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jethro_Tull_(band) "Jethro Tull (band)"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)"), [East of Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_Eden_(British_band) "East of Eden (British band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator") and [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoppo2014[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_December_2016]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears.
