Please help [improve it](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit) by checking for citation inaccuracies and resourcing or removing material failing verification._(March 2016)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | According to [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"): "Prog-rock began to emerge out of the British psychedelic scene in 1967, specifically a strain of classical/symphonic rock led by [the Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nice "The Nice"), [Procol Harum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procol_Harum "Procol Harum"), and [the Moody Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moody_Blues "The Moody Blues") ( _[Days of Future Passed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days_of_Future_Passed "Days of Future Passed")_)."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) The availability of newly affordable recording equipment coincided with the rise of a London [underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_(British_subculture) "Underground (British subculture)") scene at which the psychedelic drug LSD was commonly used. Pink Floyd and [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") functioned as [house bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_band "House band") at all-night events at locations such as [Middle Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Earth_(club) "Middle Earth (club)") and the [UFO Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_Club "UFO Club"), where they experimented with sound textures and long-form songs.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004114%E2%80%9315-71)[\[nb 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-74) Many psychedelic, folk rock and early progressive bands were aided by exposure from [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1") DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004119-75) [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), who rose to prominence in the London scene and recorded with a band of English musicians, initiated the trend towards guitar virtuosity and eccentricity in rock music.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998164%E2%80%9365-76) The Scottish band 1-2-3, later renamed [Clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clouds_(60s_rock_band) "Clouds (60s rock band)"), were formed in 1966 and began performing at London clubs a year later. According to _Mojo_'s George Knemeyer: "some claim \[that they\] had a vital influence on prog-rockers such as Yes, The Nice and Family."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHogg1994-77) Symphonic rock artists in the late 1960s had some chart success, including the singles " [Nights in White Satin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nights_in_White_Satin "Nights in White Satin")" (the Moody Blues, 1967) and " [A Whiter Shade of Pale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Whiter_Shade_of_Pale "A Whiter Shade of Pale")" (Procol Harum, 1967).[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FowlesWade2012-78) The Moody Blues established the popularity of symphonic rock when they recorded _Days of Future Passed_ together with the [London Festival Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Festival_Orchestra "London Festival Orchestra").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) Classical influences sometimes took the form of pieces adapted from or inspired by classical works, such as [Jeff Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck "Jeff Beck")'s _[Beck's Bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beck's_Bolero "Beck's Bolero")_, [Love Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Sculpture "Love Sculpture")'s[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-80) [_Farandole (Arlésienne Suite No 2. Movement 4)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Arl%C3%A9sienne_(Bizet) "L'Arlésienne (Bizet)") and parts of the Nice's _[Ars Longa Vita Brevis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Longa_Vita_Brevis_(album) "Ars Longa Vita Brevis (album)")_. The latter, along with such tracks as " [Rondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Rondo_%C3%A0_la_Turk "Blue Rondo à la Turk")" and " [America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_(West_Side_Story_song) "America (West Side Story song)")", reflect a greater interest in music that is entirely instrumental. _Sgt. Pepper's_ and _Days_ both represent a growing tendency towards [song cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_cycle "Song cycle") and suites made up of multiple [movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_(music) "Movement (music)").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) [Focus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_(band) "Focus (band)") incorporated and articulated jazz-style chords, and irregular off-beat drumming into their later rock-based riffs, and several bands that included jazz-style [horn sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_section "Horn section") appeared, including [Blood, Sweat & Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood,_Sweat_&_Tears "Blood, Sweat & Tears") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(band) "Chicago (band)"). Of these, Martin highlights Chicago in particular for their experimentation with suites and extended compositions, such as the " [Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_for_a_Girl_in_Buchannon "Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon")" on _[Chicago II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(album) "Chicago (album)")_.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998163%E2%80%93164-81) Jazz influences appeared in the music of British bands such as [Traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_(band) "Traffic (band)"), [Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum_(band) "Colosseum (band)") and [If](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_(band) "If (band)"), together with [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene") bands such as [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") and [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)"). Canterbury scene bands emphasised the use of wind instruments, complex chord changes and long improvisations.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199720-82) Martin writes that in 1968, "full-blown progressive rock" was not yet in existence; however, albums were released by three bands who would later come to the forefront of the music: Jethro Tull, Caravan and Soft Machine.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998168-83) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["The Court of the Crimson King" (1969)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_The_Court_of_the_Crimson_King.ogg "File:King Crimson - The Court of the Crimson King.ogg") Macan writes that King Crimson's album "displays every element of the mature progressive rock genre... \[and\] exerted a powerful extramusical influence on later progressive rock bands".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84) * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ The term "progressive rock", which appeared in the liner notes of Caravan's 1968 [self-titled debut LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(Caravan_album) "Caravan (Caravan album)"), came to be applied to bands that used classical music techniques to expand the styles and concepts available to rock music.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199726-85)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowman2001184-86) The Nice, the Moody Blues, Procol Harum and Pink Floyd all contained elements of what is now called progressive rock, but none represented as complete an example of the genre as several bands that formed soon after.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199722%E2%80%9323-87) Almost all of the genre's major bands, including Jethro Tull, King Crimson, Yes, [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator"), [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Gentle Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentle_Giant "Gentle Giant"), [Barclay James Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclay_James_Harvest "Barclay James Harvest") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), released their debut albums during the years 1968–1970. Most of these were folk-rock albums that gave little indication of what the bands' mature sound would become, but King Crimson's _[In the Court of the Crimson King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Court_of_the_Crimson_King "In the Court of the Crimson King")_ (1969) and Yes' [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(Yes_album) "Yes (Yes album)") (1969) were early, fully formed examples of the genre.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84)[\[nb 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-88) ### 1970s–1980s #### Peak years (1971–1976) See also: [Krautrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrock "Krautrock") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg/500px-DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg) [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") performing _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_ (1973), the best-selling album of the entire progressive rock period[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriore200579-89) Most of the genre's major bands released their most critically acclaimed albums during the years 1971–1976.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199727-90) The genre experienced a high degree of commercial success during the early 1970s. Between them, the bands Jethro Tull, [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [the Moody Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moody_Blues "The Moody Blues"), Yes, and Pink Floyd had five albums that reached number one in the US charts, and sixteen that reached the top ten.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199728-91)[\[nb 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-96) [Mike Oldfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Oldfield "Mike Oldfield")'s _[Tubular Bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubular_Bells "Tubular Bells")_ (1973), an excerpt of which was used as the theme for the film _[The Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")_, sold 16 million copies.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-97) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg/500px-Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer_01.jpg) [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer") were one of the most commercially successful progressive rock bands of the 1970s. They are seen here performing in 1992. Progressive rock came to be appreciated overseas, but it mostly remained a European, and especially British, phenomenon. Few American bands engaged in it, and the purest representatives of the genre, such as [Starcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starcastle "Starcastle") and [Happy the Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_the_Man "Happy the Man"), remained limited to their own geographic regions.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997185-6-98) This is at least in part due to music industry differences between the US and Great Britain.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65)[\[nb 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-101) Cultural factors were also involved, as Many of these groups were very influential even among bands that had little enthusiasm for the symphonic variety of progressive rock.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200282-124) ##### Avant-prog See also: [Zeuhl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeuhl "Zeuhl") **Avant-prog** (originally known as **avant-garde progressive rock** or **experimental prog**) is a subgenre of progressive rock that emerged in the 1970s. Times")_ calls Wonder's mid-1970s albums "prog soul of the highest order, pushing the form yet always heartfelt, ambitious and listenable".[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-129) #### Decline and fragmentation See also: [Punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") and [Symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop") Political and social trends of the late 1970s shifted away from the early 1970s [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") attitudes that had led to the genre's development and popularity. The rise in [punk cynicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_ideologies "Punk ideologies") made the utopian ideals expressed in progressive rock lyrics unfashionable.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200278-130) Virtuosity was rejected, as the expense of purchasing quality instruments and the time investment of learning to play them were seen as barriers to rock's energy and immediacy.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002115-131) There were also changes in the music industry, as record companies disappeared and merged into large [media conglomerates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_conglomerates "Media conglomerates"). Promoting and developing experimental music was not part of the [marketing strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_strategy "Marketing strategy") for these large corporations, who focused their attention on identifying and targeting profitable [market niches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niche_market "Niche market").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002108%E2%80%93110-132) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Robert_Fripp_2.jpg/500px-Robert_Fripp_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Fripp_2.jpg) King Crimson's [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp") believed that the prog movement had gone "tragically off course".[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Four of progressive rock's most successful bands – King Crimson, Yes, ELP and Genesis – went on hiatus or experienced major personnel changes during the mid-1970s.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Macan notes the September 1974 breakup of King Crimson as particularly significant, noting that Fripp (much later) referred to 1974 as the point when "all English bands in the genre should have ceased to exist".[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997179-134) More of the major bands, including Van der Graaf Generator, Gentle Giant and [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)"), dissolved between 1978 and 1980.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187%E2%80%93188-135) Many bands had by the mid-1970s reached the limit of how far they could experiment in a rock context, and fans had wearied of the extended, epic compositions. The sounds of the [Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), [Minimoog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog "Minimoog") and [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") had been thoroughly explored, and their use became clichéd. Those bands who continued to record often simplified their sound, and the genre fragmented from the late 1970s onwards.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997181%E2%80%93183-136) In [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp")'s opinion, once "progressive rock" ceased to cover new ground – becoming a set of conventions to be repeated and imitated – the genre's premise had ceased to be "progressive".[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997206-137) The era of record labels investing in their artists, giving them freedom to experiment and limited control over their content and marketing ended with the late 1970s.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016202-138) Corporate [artists and repertoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") staff exerted an increasing amount of control over the creative process that had previously belonged to the artists,[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1996188-139) and established acts were pressured to create music with simpler harmony and song structures and fewer changes in meter. A number of symphonic pop bands, such as [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc"), [the Alan Parsons Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Alan_Parsons_Project "The Alan Parsons Project") and the [Electric Light Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra"), brought the orchestral-style arrangements into a context that emphasised pop singles while allowing for occasional instances of exploration. Jethro Tull, Gentle Giant and Pink Floyd opted for a harder sound in the style of [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187-5) Few new progressive rock bands formed during this era, and those who did found that record labels were not interested in signing them.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) The short-lived supergroup U.K. was a notable exception since its members had established reputations; they produced two albums that were stylistically similar to previous artists and did little to advance the genre.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997183-141) Part of the genre's legacy in this period was its influence on other styles, as several European guitarists brought a progressive rock approach to [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") and laid the groundwork for [progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal"). [Michael Schenker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schenker "Michael Schenker"), of [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_(band) "UFO (band)"); and [Uli Jon Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uli_Jon_Roth "Uli Jon Roth"), who replaced Schenker in [Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpions_(band) "Scorpions (band)"), expanded the modal vocabulary available to guitarists.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackett2001-142)\[ _[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] Roth studied classical music with the intent of using the guitar in the way that classical composers used the violin.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress2007-143) Finally, the Dutch-born and classically trained [Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Van_Halen "Alex Van Halen") and [Eddie Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Van_Halen "Eddie Van Halen") formed [Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen "Van Halen"), featuring ground-breaking whammy-bar, tapping and cross-picking guitar performances[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress1993-144) that influenced " [shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shred_guitar "Shred guitar")" music in the 1980s.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-145) ##### Commercialisation > By the early 1980s, progressive rock was thought to be all but dead as a style, an idea reinforced by the fact that some of the principal progressive groups had developed a more commercial sound. ... What went out of the music of these now ex-progressive groups ... was any significant evocation of art music. —John Covach[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Some established artists moved towards music that was simpler and more commercially viable.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011182-146)\[ _[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\][\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Arena rock bands like [Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(band) "Journey (band)"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_(band) "Kansas (band)"), [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx_(band) "Styx (band)"), [GTR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTR_(band) "GTR (band)"), [ELO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra") and [Foreigner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreigner_(band) "Foreigner (band)") either had begun as progressive rock bands or included members with strong ties to the genre. These groups retained some of the song complexity and orchestral-style arrangements, but they moved away from lyrical mysticism in favour of more conventional themes such as relationships.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011181%E2%80%93182-147) These radio-friendly groups have been called "prog lite".[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECateforis2011154%E2%80%93159-148) Genesis transformed into a successful pop act, the prog supergroup [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(band) "Asia (band)") (consisting of members of Yes, King Crimson, and ELP) scored a number-one album in 1982,[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-149) and a re-formed Yes released the relatively mainstream _[90125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90125_(album) "90125 (album)")_ (1983), which yielded their only US number-one single, " [Owner of a Lonely Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owner_of_a_Lonely_Heart "Owner of a Lonely Heart")". (band)").[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-184)[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-185) Most of the genre's major acts released debut albums between 1983 and 1985 and shared the same manager, Keith Goodwin, a publicist who had been instrumental in promoting progressive rock during the 1970s.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997198-186) The previous decade's bands had the advantage of appearing during a prominent [countercultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture "Counterculture") movement that provided them with a large potential audience, but the neo-prog bands were limited to a relatively niche demographic and found it difficult to attract a following. Only Marillion[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997200%E2%80%9301-187) and [Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga_(band) "Saga (band)")[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark2012-188) experienced international success. Neo-prog bands tended to use [Peter Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel "Peter Gabriel")-era [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)") as their "principal model".[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-189) They were also influenced by [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") and [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock").[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERomano2010[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid2lVMAgAAQBAJpgPT390_%22Marillion%22]-190) The genre's most successful band, Marillion, suffered particularly from accusations of similarity to Genesis, although they used a different vocal style, incorporated more hard rock elements,[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011187%E2%80%93188-191) and were very influenced by bands including [Camel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camel_(band) "Camel (band)") and Pink Floyd.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-192)[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-193) Authors [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell have pointed out that the neo-prog bands were not so much plagiarising progressive rock as they were creating a new style from progressive rock elements, just as the bands of a decade before had created a new style from jazz and classical elements.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011184-194) Author Edward Macan counters by pointing out that these bands were at least partially motivated by a nostalgic desire to preserve a past style rather than a drive to innovate.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997197-195) ### 1990s–2000s #### Third wave [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Porcupine_Tree_%40_Poznan%2C_Poland_2007_04.jpg/500px-Porcupine_Tree_%40_Poznan%2C_Poland_2007_04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porcupine_Tree_@_Poznan,_Poland_2007_04.jpg) [Porcupine Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcupine_Tree "Porcupine Tree") performing in 2007 A third wave of progressive rock bands, who can also be described as a second generation of neo-prog bands,[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011199-181) emerged in the 1990s. The use of the term "progressive" to describe groups that follow in the style of bands from ten to twenty years earlier is somewhat controversial, as it has been seen as a contradiction of the spirit of experimentation and progress.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196)[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201119-197) These new bands were aided in part by the availability of personal computer-based [recording studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_audio_workstation "Digital audio workstation"), which reduced album production expenses, and the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet"), which made it easier for bands outside of the mainstream to reach widespread audiences.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnick2003-198) Record stores specialising in progressive rock appeared in large cities.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196) The [shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shred_guitar "Shred guitar") music of the 1980s was a major influence on the progressive rock groups of the 1990s.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196) Some of the newer bands, such as [the Flower Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flower_Kings "The Flower Kings"), [Spock's Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spock's_Beard "Spock's Beard") and [Glass Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_Hammer "Glass Hammer"), played a 1970s-style symphonic prog, but with an updated sound.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucky200047,127-199) A number of them began to explore the limits of the CD in the way that earlier groups had stretched the limits of the vinyl LP.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011200-200) #### Progressive metal Main article: [Progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["A Change of Seasons" by Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dream_Theater_-_A_Change_of_Seasons_(excerpt).ogg "File:Dream Theater - A Change of Seasons (excerpt).ogg") A multipart suite by Dream Theater that combines elements of progressive rock and heavy metal * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Progressive rock and [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") have similar timelines. Both emerged from late-1960s psychedelia to achieve great early-1970s success despite a lack of radio airplay and support from critics, then faded in the mid-to-late 1970s and experienced revivals in the early 1980s. Each genre experienced a fragmentation of styles at this time, and many metal bands from the [new wave of British heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_of_British_heavy_metal "New wave of British heavy metal") – most notably [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden") – onwards displayed progressive rock influences.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011259%E2%80%93260-201) [Progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") reached a point of maturity with [Queensrÿche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensr%C3%BFche "Queensrÿche")'s 1988 concept album _[Operation: Mindcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation:_Mindcrime "Operation: Mindcrime"),_ [Voivod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voivod_(band) "Voivod (band)")'s 1989 _[Nothingface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothingface_(Voivod_album) "Nothingface (Voivod album)")_, which featured abstract lyrics and a King Crimson-like texture, and [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater")'s 1992 _[Images and Words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Images_and_Words "Images and Words")_.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011260%E2%80%93262-202) Progressive rock elements appear in other metal subgenres. [Death metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_metal "Death metal")'s [guttural vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_growl "Death growl") are sometimes used by bands who can be classified as progressive, such as [Mastodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon_(band) "Mastodon (band)"), [Mudvayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudvayne "Mudvayne") and [Opeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opeth "Opeth").[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011264,_266-203) [Symphonic metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_metal "Symphonic metal") is an extension of the tendency towards orchestral passages in early progressive rock.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011266%E2%80%93267-204) Progressive rock has also served as a key inspiration for genres such as [post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock "Post-rock"),[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-allen-205) [post-metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-metal "Post-metal") and [avant-garde metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_metal "Avant-garde metal"),[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-caramanica-206) [math rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Math_rock "Math rock"),[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tudor-207) [power metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_metal "Power metal") and [neo-classical metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-classical_metal "Neo-classical metal").[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-miers-208) #### New prog Not to be confused with [Neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"). **New prog** describes the wave of progressive rock bands in the 2000s who revived the genre. According to _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_'s Evan Serpick, "success stories like [System of a Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_a_Down "System of a Down") and up-and-comers like the [Dillinger Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillinger_Escape_Plan "Dillinger Escape Plan"), [Lightning Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_Bolt_(band) "Lightning Bolt (band)"), [Coheed and Cambria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coheed_and_Cambria "Coheed and Cambria"), and [the Mars Volta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mars_Volta "The Mars Volta") create incredibly complex and inventive music that sounds like a heavier, more aggressive version of '70s behemoths such as Led Zeppelin and King Crimson."[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-209) #### Wider influence The turn of the millennium also saw the rise of a number of bands to mainstream success who, whilst not explicitly identifying as progressive rock, have incorporated influences from it and embraced an experimentalism and complexity in their music which has been regarded as being in keeping with the genre's traditions. [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead") have been embraced by some progressive rock fans and musicians, with Rush's [Geddy Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geddy_Lee "Geddy Lee") declaring _[OK Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OK_Computer "OK Computer")_ as one of his favourite albums and arguing that they carried on the torch from bands like Yes and Genesis. Radiohead's drummer [Philip Selway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Selway "Philip Selway") has cited King Crimson and Pink Floyd as influences, and the band's eclectic and experimental style has drawn on a range of sources, including jazz, electronic music, art rock, krautrock, post-rock and the work of [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart").[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-210) [Tool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tool_(band) "Tool (band)") and King Crimson have acknowledged each other as influences and toured together.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-211)[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-212)[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-213) Other bands embracing progressive influences include [Muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse_(band) "Muse (band)")[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-214) and [Mansun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansun "Mansun"), whose second album _[Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_(Mansun_album) "Six (Mansun album)")_ has been listed as a favourite British rock album of Porcupine Tree's [Steven Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Wilson "Steven Wilson"), who has collaborated and toured with former Mansun frontman [Paul Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Draper_(musician) "Paul Draper (musician)").[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-215)[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-216)[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-217) Ween's 1997 album _[The Mollusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mollusk "The Mollusk")_ has also been noted for its progressive rock influences, complete with [Storm Thorgerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Thorgerson "Storm Thorgerson")-designed cover art.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-218) ### 2010s–2020s The Progressive Music Awards were launched in 2012 by the British magazine _[Prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prog_(magazine) "Prog (magazine)")_ to honour the genre's established acts and to promote its newer bands. In 2019, the Prog Report named [Mike Portnoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Portnoy "Mike Portnoy") and [Neal Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Morse "Neal Morse") artists of the decade for 2010–2019. During this time, Portnoy released 40 albums, 24 of them with Morse, while Morse released an additional 5 albums of his own.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-219) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") in 2020, the Prog Report launched a virtual concert, _Prog From Home_, bringing together many of the biggest artists active in the genre.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-220) On April 3, 2022, "The Alien" won a [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") for [Best Metal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Metal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance"), giving [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater") their first Grammy.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-221) ## Festivals Many prominent progressive rock bands got their initial exposure at large [rock festivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_festival "Rock festival") that were held in Britain during the late 1960s and early 1970s. King Crimson made their first major appearance at the [1969 Hyde Park free concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stones_in_the_Park "Stones in the Park"), before a crowd estimated to be as large as 650,000, in support of [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones").[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFripp1975-222) Emerson, Lake & Palmer debuted at the [1970 Isle of Wight Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival_1970 "Isle of Wight Festival 1970"), at which [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)") and Jethro Tull also appeared.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150%E2%80%9351-223) Jethro Tull were also present at the 1969 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), the first year in which that festival invited rock bands to perform. [Hawkwind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkwind "Hawkwind") appeared at many British festivals throughout the 1970s, although they sometimes showed up uninvited, set up a stage on the periphery of the event, and played for free.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150-224) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Supertramp0062.jpg/500px-Supertramp0062.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Supertramp0062.jpg) Supertramp performing in 1979[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg/500px-King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_(01).jpg) [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") performing at the Dour Festival, 2003 Renewed interest in the genre in the 1990s led to the development of progressive rock festivals.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196) ProgFest, organised by Greg Walker and David Overstreet in 1993, was first held in [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA")'s Royce Hall,[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) and featured Sweden's Änglagård, the UK's IQ, Quill and Citadel. CalProg was held annually in Whittier, California during the early 2000s.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-226) The North East Art Rock Festival, or [NEARfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEARfest "NEARfest"),[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnick2003-198) held its first event in 1999 in [Bethlehem, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem,_Pennsylvania "Bethlehem, Pennsylvania") and held annual sold-out concerts until 2012's NEARfest Apocalypse, which featured headliners [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)") and Renaissance.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012e-227) Other festivals include the annual ProgDay (the longest-running and only outdoor progressive music festival) in [Chapel Hill, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_Hill,_North_Carolina "Chapel Hill, North Carolina"); the annual Rites of Spring Festival (RoSfest) in [Sarasota, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarasota,_Florida "Sarasota, Florida"); [The Rogue Independent Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rogue_Independent_Music_Festival "The Rogue Independent Music Festival") in Atlanta, Georgia; [Baja Prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baja_Prog "Baja Prog") in [Mexicali, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicali "Mexicali"); [ProgPower USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_USA "ProgPower USA") in Atlanta, Georgia; [ProgPower Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_Europe "ProgPower Europe") in [Baarlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baarlo "Baarlo"), Netherlands; and ProgStock in Rahway, NJ, which held its first event in 2017.[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-228) Another popular prog festival is Cruise to the Edge; 2026's line-up included [Marillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marillion "Marillion"), [Steven Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hackett "Steve Hackett"), and [Big Big Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Big_Train "Big Big Train").[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-229) ## Reception The genre has received both critical acclaim and criticism throughout the years. Progressive rock has been described as parallel to the classical music of [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky") and [Béla Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók").[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) This desire to expand the boundaries of rock, combined with some musicians' dismissiveness toward mainstream rock and pop, dismayed critics and led to accusations of elitism. Its intellectual, fantastic and apolitical lyrics, and shunning of rock's blues roots, were abandonments of the very things that many critics valued in rock music.[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997168%E2%80%9373-230) Progressive rock also represented the maturation of rock as a genre, but there was an opinion among critics that rock was and should remain fundamentally tied to adolescence, so rock and maturity were mutually exclusive.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002107-231) Criticisms over the complexity of their music provoked some bands to create music that was even more complex.[\[nb 15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-235) BBC radio DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel"), who was one of the first people to play progressive rock on British radio, later said "the one distinguishing feature about early-70s progressive rock was that it didn't progress".[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-236) Most of the musicians involved were male, as was the case for most rock of the time,[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011204-237) although [Annie Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Haslam "Annie Haslam") of [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)") was a notable exception. Female singers were better represented in [progressive folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_folk "Progressive folk") bands,[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997135-238) who displayed a broader range of vocal styles than the progressive rock bands[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004204-239) with whom they frequently toured and shared band members.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004131-240) British and European audiences typically followed concert hall behaviour protocols associated with classical music performances and were more reserved in their behaviour than audiences for other forms of rock. This confused musicians during US tours, as they found American audiences less attentive and more prone to outbursts during quiet passages.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997263-241) These aspirations towards [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") reflect progressive rock's origins as a music created largely by [upper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class")\- and [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class")-class, [white-collar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-collar_workers "White-collar workers"), college-educated males from [Southern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_England "Southern England"). The music never reflected the concerns of or was embraced by working-class listeners,[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997144%E2%80%9348-242) except in the US, where listeners appreciated the musicians' virtuosity.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997156-243) Progressive rock's exotic, literary topics were considered particularly irrelevant to British youth during the late 1970s, when the nation suffered from a poor economy and frequent strikes and shortages.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011163%E2%80%93164-244) Even King Crimson leader Robert Fripp dismissed progressive rock lyrics as "the philosophical meanderings of some English half-wit who is circumnavigating some inessential point of experience in his life".[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm1990-245) Bands whose darker lyrics avoided utopianism, such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Van der Graaf Generator, experienced less critical disfavour.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199778-246) In 2002, Pink Floyd guitarist [David Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gilmour "David Gilmour") said, "I wasn't a big fan of most of what you'd call progressive rock. I'm like [Groucho Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groucho_Marx "Groucho Marx"): I don't want to belong to any club that would have me for a member."[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-247) In 2014, [Peter Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel "Peter Gabriel") remarked, "Despite prog probably being the most derided musical genre of all time there were—as today—a lot of extraordinary musicians trying to break down the barriers to reject the rules of music. It was genuinely pioneering at the time. We didn't always get it right, but when it did work we could move people and get some magic happening. I see it all as a very healthy part of growing up."[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-248) [Ian Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Anderson "Ian Anderson"), the frontman of Jethro Tull, commented: > I still like the original term that comes from 1969: progressive rock – but that was with a small "p" and a small "r". Prog Rock, on the other hand, has different connotations – of grandeur and pomposity \[...\] I think looking back on it that most of it was a pretty good experience for musicians and listeners alike. Some of it was a little bit overblown, but in the case of much of the music, it was absolutely spot on.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-249) While music fans for years have declared progressive rock to be dead,[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-250) the scene is still active with many sub-genres.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-251) ## List of progressive rock artists Main article: [List of progressive rock artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_progressive_rock_artists "List of progressive rock artists") ## See also [![Wiktionary logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg/120px-Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg) Look up _**[progressive rock](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/progressive%20rock "wiktionary:progressive rock")**_ in Wiktionary, the free dictionary. - [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-15)In the rock music of the 1970s, the "art" descriptor was generally understood to mean "aggressively avant-garde" or "pretentiously progressive".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-ArtPunkMurray-14) 02. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-24)From about 1967, "pop music" was increasingly used in opposition to the term "rock music", a division that gave generic significance to both terms.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-23) 03. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-32)Formalism refers to a preoccupation with established external compositional systems, structural unity, and the autonomy of individual art works. Eclecticism, like formalism, connotes a predilection towards style synthesis, or integration. However, contrary to formalist tendencies, eclecticism foregrounds discontinuities between historical and contemporary styles and electronic media, sometimes referring simultaneously to vastly different musical genres, idioms and cultural codes. Examples include [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' " [Within You Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Within_You_Without_You "Within You Without You")" (1967) and [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix")'s 1969 version of " [The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner")".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200093-31) 04. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-43)Allan Moore writes: "It should be clear by now that, although this history appears to offer a roughly chronological succession of styles, there is no single, linear history to that thing we call _popular song_.... Sometimes it appears that there are only peripheries. Sometimes, audiences gravitate towards a centre. The most prominent period when this happened was in the early to mid 1960s when it seems that almost everyone, irrespective of age, class or cultural background, listened to the Beatles. But by 1970 this monolothic position had again broken down. Both [the Edgar Broughton Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Edgar_Broughton_Band "The Edgar Broughton Band")'s ' [Apache Dropout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Dropout?action=edit&redlink=1 "Apache Dropout")' and [Edison Lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_Lighthouse "Edison Lighthouse")'s ' [Love grows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Grows_(Where_My_Rosemary_Goes) "Love Grows (Where My Rosemary Goes)")' were released in 1970 with strong Midlands/London connections, and both were audible on the same radio stations, but were operating according to very different aesthetics."[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016199%E2%80%93200-42) 05. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-67)LP sales first overtook those of singles in 1969.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004120-66) 06. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-74)Beatles member [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon") is known to have attended at least one such event, a [happening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happening "Happening") called [the 14 Hour Technicolor Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_14_Hour_Technicolor_Dream "The 14 Hour Technicolor Dream").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Brien1999-72) [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") was deeply connected to the underground through his involvement with the [Indica Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indica_Gallery "Indica Gallery").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles1999-73) 07. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-96)Tull alone scored 11 [gold albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_album "Gold album") and 5 [platinum albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_album "Platinum album").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECleveland2005-92) Pink Floyd's 1970 album _[Atom Heart Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_Heart_Mother "Atom Heart Mother")_ reached the top spot on the UK charts. Their 1973 album _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_, which united their extended compositions with the more structured kind of composing employed when [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett") was their songwriter,[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley199234%E2%80%9335-93) spent more than two years at the top of the charts[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley19924,_38-94) and remained on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") album chart for fifteen years.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriedlander1998245-95) 09. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-101)Radio airplay was less important in the UK, where popular music recordings had limited air-time on official radio stations (as opposed to on [pirate radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_radio_in_the_United_Kingdom "Pirate radio in the United Kingdom")) until the 1967 launch of [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65) UK audiences were accustomed to hearing bands in clubs, and British bands could support themselves through touring. US audiences were first exposed to new music on the radio, and bands in the US required radio airplay for success.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987296-7-99) Radio stations were averse to progressive rock's longer-form compositions, which hampered [advertising sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_advertisement "Radio advertisement").[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-100) 10. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-113)Van der Graaf Generator were much more popular there than in their own country. Genesis were hugely successful in Continental Europe at a time when they were still limited to a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") in Britain and the US.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-spicer-112)\[ _[importance of example(s)?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Refexample#Self-sourcing "Template:Refexample")_\] 11. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-120)This can be heard in [Triumvirat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumvirat "Triumvirat"), an organ trio in the style of ELP; [Ange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ange_(band) "Ange (band)") and [Celeste](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celeste%20(gruppo%20musicale) "it:Celeste (gruppo musicale)") who have had a strong King Crimson influence.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997267-118) Others brought national elements to their style: Spain's [Triana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triana_(band) "Triana (band)") introduced [flamenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco "Flamenco") elements, groups such as the Swedish [Samla Mammas Manna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samla_Mammas_Manna "Samla Mammas Manna") drew from the folk music styles of their respective nations, and Italian bands such as [Il Balletto di Bronzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_Balletto_di_Bronzo "Il Balletto di Bronzo"), Rustichelli & Bordini, leaned towards an approach that was more overtly emotional than that of their British counterparts.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997184-119) 12. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-158)Pink Floyd were unable to repeat that combination of commercial and critical success, as their sole follow-up, _[The Final Cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Cut_(album) "The Final Cut (album)")_, was several years in coming[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997188-151) and was essentially a [Roger Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Waters "Roger Waters") solo project[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-merc-152) that consisted largely of material that had been rejected for _The Wall_.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tsmith-153) The band later reunited without Waters and restored many of the progressive elements that had been downplayed in the band's late-1970s work.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997195-154) This version of the band was very popular,[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-harrington87-155) but critical opinion of their later albums is less favourable.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-graves-156)[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-wyman-157) 13. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-164)[Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") frontman [Johnny Rotten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lydon "John Lydon") famously wore a T-shirt that read "I hate Pink Floyd",[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) but he expressed admiration for Van der Graaf Generator,[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-boros-160) Can,[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-lydon-161) and many years later, Pink Floyd themselves.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-162) [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") expressed a preference for the approach of the punk and new wave bands in New York, as he found them to be more experimental and less personality-based than the English bands.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm199530-163) 14. ​
(m.1970)​ | Musical artist **Keith Graham Tippetts** (25 August 1947 – 14 June 2020),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) known professionally as **Keith Tippett**, was a British [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer. According to [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Tippett's career "...spanned jazz-rock, [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), improvised and contemporary music, as well as modern jazz for more than half-a-century". He held "an unparallelled place in British contemporary music,"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) and was known for "his unique approach to improvisation".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) Tippett appeared and recorded in many settings, including a duet with [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), duets with his wife [Julie Tippetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Tippetts "Julie Tippetts") (née Driscoll), solo performances, and as a bandleader.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guy-3) ## Early life Born in [Southmead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southmead "Southmead"), [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol"), England,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Tippett was the son of an English father who was a policeman and an Irish mother named Kitty. He wrote music dedicated to her after she died. He was the oldest of three siblings and went to Greenway Secondary Modern school in Southmead. As a child he played piano, church organ, cornet, and tenor horn.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) At fourteen he formed his first band, KT Trad Lads, with school friends Richard Murch, Mike Milton, Terry Pratt, and Bob Chard, and Eric Condell performing traditional jazz. He formed a modern jazz trio in Bristol and played regularly at the Dugout Club in Park Row, Bristol. ## Music career In 1967, Tippett moved to London to pursue a career in music, taking menial jobs while performing in jazz clubs.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) With a scholarship he attended the Barry Summer School Jazz Course in Wales, where he met [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean"), [Nick Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Evans_(trombonist) "Nick Evans (trombonist)"), and [Marc Charig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Charig "Marc Charig") and with them started a band.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) The Keith Tippett Sextet was hired for a residency at the [100 Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Club "100 Club") in Oxford Street,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) leading to a contract with Polydor, which released their first two albums, _You Are There... I Am Here_ (1970) and _Dedicated to You, but You Weren't Listening_ (1971).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) After leaving Vertigo, Tippett formed [Centipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centipede_(band) "Centipede (band)"), a 50-piece band that included his wife [Julie Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Driscoll "Julie Driscoll"), and brought together much of a generation of young British jazz and rock musicians.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) As well as performing some concerts (limited economically by the size of the band), they recorded one double-album, _[Septober Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septober_Energy "Septober Energy")_, a Tippett composition, which was released on the [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records") label in 1971. Despite substantial publicity, the album failed to sell in sufficient numbers to justify the expense of maintaining the project.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) In early 1970, Tippett was part of a temporary [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") line-up for the recording of their second album _[In the Wake of Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Wake_of_Poseidon "In the Wake of Poseidon")_.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-7) He also contributed as a session musician to the band's subsequent two albums _[Lizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizard_(album) "Lizard (album)")_ later in 1970 and _[Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islands_(King_Crimson_album) "Islands (King Crimson album)")_ in 1971. For his next album as a leader, _Blueprint_ (1972),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) he used a smaller group comprising himself and Julie Tippetts with bassist [Roy Babbington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Babbington "Roy Babbington") and drummer Frank Perry. The band then expanded slightly to become Ovary Lodge,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) who recorded two albums, one for RCA and a second for the Ogun label. Tippett and his band also recorded in the 1970s for [Giorgio Gomelsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gomelsky "Giorgio Gomelsky")'s label, Utopia, releasing the Julie Tippetts album, _Sunset Glow_. Tippett continued to play with various combinations of musicians through the 1970s, playing improvisational jazz and [jazz-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock "Jazz-rock") with such musicians as [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Dudu Pukwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudu_Pukwana "Dudu Pukwana"), [Harry Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Miller_(jazz_bassist) "Harry Miller (jazz bassist)"), Elton Dean, [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), and [Louis Moholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Moholo "Louis Moholo").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) From 1979, he also started to release many live albums of solo piano performances, beginning with _The Unlonely Raindancer_. In the late 1980s, he, along with [Paul Dunmall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Dunmall "Paul Dunmall") saxes, Paul Rogers bass, and [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin_(drummer) "Tony Levin (drummer)") drums, formed the quartet Mujician, playing purely improvised jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Mujician released six albums between 1990 and 2002. He also formed a trio with Julie Tippetts and Willi Kellers, and wrote film and television scores. He also wrote music for [string quartets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_quartet "String quartet") and piano, and taught at summer schools. Tippett also continued to record and to tour in Britain and Europe with various ensembles. He also worked with musicians [Andy Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Sheppard "Andy Sheppard"), as well as with his frequent collaborators Elton Dean, Louis Moholo, and Howard Riley.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) In Bristol, starting in 1989 and continuing through the 1990s, he started the Seedbed Orchestra, which performed at venues including the [Thekla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Thekla "The Thekla"), the [Arnolfini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnolfini,_Bristol "Arnolfini, Bristol") and [Bristol Old Vic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Old_Vic "Bristol Old Vic").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_1-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_2-9) This enabled beginners, amateurs and professional musicians to play in a large ensemble and was "emblematic of his quest to unite music of all types in a non-elitist, open to all, friendly environment free of establishment restrictions."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_3-10) He became a "musician's musician when he first set up the Seedbed Orchestra where many Bristol musicians could benefit from his guidance."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_4-11) ## Personal life and death He married singer [Julie Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Driscoll "Julie Driscoll") in 1970. In 2018, he had a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack") and [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") but returned to performing in 2019.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) He died on 14 June 2020 at the age of 72.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) In 2026, the Authorised biography, “ Keith Tippett: Mujician”, written by Martin Phillips with a Foreword by Richard Williams, was published by Jazz In Britain. ## Discography ### As leader - _You Are Here...
