- [electric guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar")
- [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar") | **Modal jazz** is [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") that makes use of [musical modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music) "Mode (music)"), often [modulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music) "Modulation (music)") among them to accompany the [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") instead of relying on one [tonal center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonic_(music) "Tonic (music)") used across the piece. Though exerting influence to the present, modal jazz was most popular in the 1950s and 1960s, as evidenced by the success of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s 1958 composition " [Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(composition) "Milestones (composition)")" and 1959 album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s quartet from 1960 to 1965. Other performers of modal jazz include [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Essential-1) ## History In [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") as well as in [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), musicians use chords to provide the background for solos. A piece starts out with a theme that introduces a series of chords for the solos. These chords repeat throughout the whole piece, while the soloists play new, improvised themes over the repeated [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"). By the 1950s, improvising over chords had become such a dominant part of jazz that sidemen at recording dates were sometimes given nothing more than a list of chords to play from.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-2) [Mercer Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Ellington "Mercer Ellington") has stated that [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") conceived the melody to " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")" in 1936 as a result of his days studying music in Puerto Rico, where they could not afford much sheet music so the teacher would turn the music upside down after they had learned to play it right-side up.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) This "inversion" technique led to a modal sound throughout Tizol's work.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") reportedly rehearsed a small group consisting of [Harold Ousley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Ousley "Harold Ousley"), [Vernel Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernel_Fournier "Vernel Fournier"), and [Wilbur Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ware "Wilbur Ware") in 1950 that played original songs that were modal in which the melody was based on a single chord or [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato#Vamp "Ostinato") – ten years before this approach became popular in jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-4) Saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") has noted that the 1953 composition " [Glass Enclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_Enclosure "Glass Enclosure")" by pianist Bud Powell was one of the earliest jazz compositions to make use of [Lydian chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_chord "Lydian chord"), based on the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode") that was not widely used in jazz until about a decade later.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-5) Powell's 1951 [Un Poco Loco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un_Poco_Loco "Un Poco Loco") uses the Lydian chords and even uses Lydian chords stacked on top of each implying a [polytonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality") (D [major 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_seventh_chord "Major seventh chord") over C major 7: CEGBDF#AC#) with the improvisation based on alternating Lydian-ish polytonality and an [altered dominant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_dominant "Altered dominant") chord.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-6) Towards the end of the 1950s, spurred by the experiments of composer and bandleader George Russell, musicians began using a modal approach. They chose not to write their pieces using conventional chord changes, but instead using modes. Musicians employing this technique include Miles Davis, [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), Bill Evans, [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and Wayne Shorter. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png/500px-Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png) Opening chord to " [Maiden Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_Voyage_(composition) "Maiden Voyage (composition)")": minor [eleventh chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleventh_chord "Eleventh chord") (Am9/D).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-What-7)[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9e/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid "File:Minor eleventh chord Herbie Hancock Maiden Voyage.mid") Using D [Dorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode#Modern_Dorian_mode "Dorian mode").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-8) Among the significant compositions of modal jazz were " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(composition) "So What (composition)")" by Miles Davis and " [Impressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressions_(composition) "Impressions (composition)")" by John Coltrane.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) "So What" and "Impressions" follow the same AABA structure and were in D Dorian for the A sections and modulated a half step up to E-flat Dorian for the B section. The [Dorian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode "Dorian mode") is the [natural minor scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_scale#Natural_minor "Minor scale") with a raised sixth. Other compositions include Davis's " [Flamenco Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco_Sketches "Flamenco Sketches")", Bill Evans's " [Peace Piece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Piece "Peace Piece")", and Shorter's " [Footprints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footprints_(composition) "Footprints (composition)")".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) Davis recorded one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time in this modal framework. _Kind of Blue_ is an exploration of the possibilities of modal jazz.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Complete-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) Although his explorations of modal jazz were sporadic throughout the 1960s, he included several of the tunes from _Kind of Blue_ in the repertoire of his second quintet. Coltrane took the lead in extensively exploring the limits of modal improvisation and composition with his quartet, featuring [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") (drums), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner") (piano), and [Reggie Workman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Workman "Reggie Workman") and [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") (bass). Several of Coltrane's albums from the period are recognized as examples of modal jazz: _[Africa/Brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa/Brass "Africa/Brass")_ (1961),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) _[Live! at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live!_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Live! at the Village Vanguard")_ (1962), _[Crescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescent_(John_Coltrane) "Crescent (John Coltrane)")_ (1964), _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1964),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) and _[Meditations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_(John_Coltrane_album) "Meditations (John Coltrane album)")_ (1965). Coltrane's compositions from this period such as "India", "Chasin' the Trane", "Crescent", and "Impressions" have entered the jazz repertoire, along with his interpretations of standards like Richard Rodgers's " [My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(song) "My Favorite Things (song)")", and the traditional " [Greensleeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensleeves "Greensleeves")". ## References 01. (m.1954;div.1964)​ | Musical artist **Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman** (March 9, 1930 – June 11, 2015)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist, trumpeter, violinist, and composer. He is best known as a principal founder of the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") genre, a term derived from his 1960 album _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. His pioneering works often abandoned the [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony")-based composition, [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), chord changes, and fixed rhythm found in earlier jazz idioms;[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-2) instead, Coleman emphasized an experimental approach to [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") rooted in ensemble playing and [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") phrasing.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Thom Jurek of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called him "one of the most beloved and polarizing figures in jazz history", noting that while "now celebrated as a fearless innovator and a genius, he was initially regarded by peers and critics as rebellious, disruptive, and even a fraud."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Born and raised in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), Coleman taught himself to play the saxophone when he was a teenager.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) He began his musical career playing in local [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") groups and eventually formed his own jazz group in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), featuring members such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"). In November 1959, his quartet began a controversial residency at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in New York City and he released the influential album _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Coleman's subsequent Atlantic releases in the early 1960s would profoundly impact the direction of jazz in that decade, and his compositions " [Lonely Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Woman_(composition) "Lonely Woman (composition)")" and " [Broadway Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Blues_(Coleman) "Broadway Blues (Coleman)")" became [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") cited as important early works in free jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-HellmerLawn2005-4) In the mid 1960s, Coleman left Atlantic for other labels, including [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and began performing with his young son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums. He explored symphonic composition with his 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_, featuring the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). In the mid-1970s, he formed the group [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), which performed electric [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and elaborated on his theory of [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) In 1995, he and Denardo founded the [Harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics#Record_label "Harmolodics") record label. Coleman's 2006 album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_ received the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Music "Pulitzer Prize for Music"), making him the second jazz musician ever to receive the honor.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-5) ## Biography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Biography")\] ### Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early life")\] Coleman was born Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman on March 9, 1930, in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fordham-6) where he was raised.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Atlantic1972-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EGP-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) He attended [I.M. Terrell High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Terrell_High_School "I.M. Terrell High School") in Fort Worth, where he participated in the band program until he was dismissed for improvising during [John Philip Sousa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Sousa "John Philip Sousa")'s march " [The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post_(march) "The Washington Post (march)")". He began performing [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") on tenor saxophone, and formed The Jam Jivers with [Prince Lasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Lasha "Prince Lasha") and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg) Coleman playing his signature alto saxophone in 1971 Eager to leave town, he accepted a job in 1949 with a [Silas Green from New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silas_Green_from_New_Orleans "Silas Green from New Orleans") traveling show and then with touring rhythm and blues shows. After a show in [Baton Rouge, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana "Baton Rouge, Louisiana"), he was assaulted and his saxophone was destroyed.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Spellman-10) Coleman subsequently switched to alto saxophone, first playing it in New Orleans after the Baton Rouge incident; the alto would remain his primary instrument for the rest of his life. He then joined the band of [Pee Wee Crayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pee_Wee_Crayton "Pee Wee Crayton") and traveled with them to Los Angeles. He worked at various jobs in Los Angeles, including as an elevator operator, while pursuing his music career.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-11) Coleman found like-minded musicians in Los Angeles, such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Bobby Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Bradford "Bobby Bradford"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"), and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EJN-12) Thanks to the intercession of friends and a successful audition, Ornette signed his first recording contract with Los Angeles-based [Contemporary Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records "Contemporary Records"),[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-13) which allowed him to sell the tracks from his debut album, _[Something Else!!!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something_Else!!!! "Something Else!!!!")_ (1958), with Cherry, Higgins, [Walter Norris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Norris "Walter Norris"), and [Don Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Payne_(musician) "Don Payne (musician)").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Jurek-14) During the same year, he briefly belonged to a quintet led by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley") that performed at a club in Los Angeles. (That band is recorded on _[Live at the Hilcrest Club 1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_the_Hilcrest_Club_1958 "Live at the Hilcrest Club 1958")._)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) By the time _[Tomorrow Is the Question!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question! "Tomorrow Is the Question!")_ was recorded soon after with Cherry, bassists [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath") and [Red Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Mitchell "Red Mitchell"), and drummer [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"), the jazz world had been shaken up by Coleman's music. Some jazz musicians called him a fraud, while conductor and composer [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") praised him.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EJN-12) ### 1959: _The Shape of Jazz to Come_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: 1959: The Shape of Jazz to Come")\] In 1959, [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") released Coleman's third studio album, _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_. According to music critic Steve Huey, the album "was a watershed event in the genesis of avant-garde jazz, profoundly steering its future course and throwing down a gauntlet that some still haven't come to grips with".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Huey-15) _[Jazzwise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazzwise "Jazzwise")_ magazine listed it at number three on their list of the 100 best jazz albums of all time in 2017.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Flynn-16) Coleman's quartet received a long and sometimes controversial engagement at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York City. Leonard Bernstein, [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton"), and the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet") were impressed and offered encouragement. Hampton asked to perform with the quartet, while Bernstein helped Haden obtain a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") grant. A young [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed") followed Coleman's quartet around New York City.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-:0-17) Among detractors, [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") said that Coleman was "all screwed up inside",[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Roberts-19) although he later became a proponent of Coleman's innovations;[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Kahn-20) [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") remarked of Coleman that "I don't know what he's playing, but it's not jazz."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-:0-17) Coleman's early sound was due in part to his use of a plastic [Grafton saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafton_saxophone "Grafton saxophone"), which he had purchased in Los Angeles in 1954 because he was unable to afford a metal saxophone at the time.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) On his Atlantic recordings, Coleman's sidemen were Cherry on cornet or [pocket trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_trumpet "Pocket trumpet"); Charlie Haden, [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro"), and then [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") on bass; and Higgins or [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell") on drums. Coleman's complete recordings for the label were collected on the box set _[Beauty Is a Rare Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_a_Rare_Thing "Beauty Is a Rare Thing")_ in 1993.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Yanow-21) ### 1960s: _Free Jazz_ and Blue Note \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1960s: Free Jazz and Blue Note")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg) Coleman playing the trumpet at the [Great American Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Music_Hall "Great American Music Hall"), [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), in 1981 In 1960, Coleman recorded _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_, which featured a "double quartet" including Cherry and [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") on trumpet, [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy") on bass clarinet, Haden and LaFaro on bass, and Higgins and Blackwell on drums.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-rhino-22) The album was recorded in stereo, with one woodwind/trumpet/bass/drums quartet in each channel. _Free Jazz_ was, at 37 minutes, the longest recorded continuous jazz performance at the time[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-23) and was one of Coleman's most controversial albums.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-24) The January 18, 1962, issue of _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine presented an article entitled "Double View of a Double Quartet" in which Pete Welding gave the album five stars while John A. Tynan rated it zero stars.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Welding-25) While Coleman had intended "free jazz" as simply an album title, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") was soon considered a new genre; Coleman expressed discomfort with the term.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Reich2010-26) After he left Atlantic, Coleman's music became more angular and engaged with the [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") which had developed in part around his innovations.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Yanow-21) He formed a trio with bassist [David Izenzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Izenzon "David Izenzon") and drummer [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett") and began playing trumpet and violin in addition to the saxophone. His friendship with free jazz saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") influenced his unorthodox self-taught style on the trumpet and violin. Charlie Haden sometimes joined this trio to form a two-bass quartet. In 1966, Coleman signed with [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and released the two-volume live album _[At the "Golden Circle" Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_%22Golden_Circle%22_Stockholm "At the \"Golden Circle\" Stockholm")_ featuring Izenzon and Moffett, recorded in Sweden the previous December.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Freeman-27) Later that year, he recorded _[The Empty Foxhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empty_Foxhole "The Empty Foxhole")_ with Haden on bass and his ten year-old son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums;[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_2015-28) [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") and [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne") regarded Denardo's appearance on the album as an ill-advised publicity stunt.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Gabel-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Spencer-30) Denardo later became his father's primary drummer in the late 1970s. Coleman formed another quartet with Haden, Garrison, and [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones"), and [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") joined the group, usually on tenor saxophone. On February 29, 1968, Coleman's quartet (with Haden, Izenzon, and Ed Blackwell) performed live with [Yoko Ono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoko_Ono "Yoko Ono") at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall"), and a recording from their rehearsal was subsequently included on Ono's 1970 album _[Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoko_Ono/Plastic_Ono_Band "Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band")_ as the track "AOS".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Chrispell-31) He explored his interest in string textures on _[Town Hall, 1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Hall,_1962 "Town Hall, 1962")_, culminating in the 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_ with the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). ### 1970s–1990s: Harmolodic funk and Prime Time \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 1970s–1990s: Harmolodic funk and Prime Time")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg/250px-Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg) Coleman playing the violin with Prime Time in 1978, flanked by guitarists Charlie Ellerbee (left) and [Bern Nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern_Nix "Bern Nix") (right) Coleman, like Miles Davis before him, soon took to playing with electric instruments and incorporating [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") influences. The 1976 album _[Dancing in Your Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_in_Your_Head "Dancing in Your Head")_, Coleman's first recording with the group which later became known as [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), prominently featured bass guitarist [Jamaaladeen Tacuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaaladeen_Tacuma "Jamaaladeen Tacuma") and electric guitarists [Bern Nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern_Nix "Bern Nix") and Charlie Ellerbee. While this marked a stylistic departure for Coleman, the music retained aspects of what he called [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics") _._ Coleman's subsequent albums with Prime Time, such as _[Virgin Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Beauty "Virgin Beauty")_ and _[Of Human Feelings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Human_Feelings "Of Human Feelings")_, continued to use rock and funk rhythms in a style sometimes called [free funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_funk "Free funk").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-33) [Jerry Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Garcia "Jerry Garcia") of the [Grateful Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grateful_Dead "Grateful Dead") played guitar on three tracks on _Virgin Beauty_: "Three Wishes", "Singing in the Shower", and "Desert Players". Coleman later joined the Grateful Dead on stage at a 1993 performance in [Oakland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Deadbase-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-35) In December 1985, Coleman and guitarist [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny") recorded _[Song X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_X "Song X")_ with Haden, Denardo Coleman, and second drummer [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg/250px-Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg) Coleman performing in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") in 1982 In 1990, [Reggio Emilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Emilia "Reggio Emilia"), Italy, held a three-day "Portrait of the Artist" festival in Coleman's honor, in which he performed with Cherry, Haden, and Higgins. The festival also presented performances of his chamber music and _Skies of America_.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-36) In 1991, Coleman played on the soundtrack of [David Cronenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cronenberg "David Cronenberg")'s film _[Naked Lunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_Lunch_(film) "Naked Lunch (film)")_; the orchestra was conducted by [Howard Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Shore "Howard Shore").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-37)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-38) Coleman released four records in 1995 and 1996, and for the first time in many years worked regularly with piano players ( [Geri Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_Allen "Geri Allen") and [Joachim Kühn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_K%C3%BChn "Joachim Kühn")). ### 2000s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: 2000s")\] Two 1972 Coleman recordings, "Happy House" and "Foreigner in a Free Land", were used in [Gus Van Sant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gus_Van_Sant "Gus Van Sant")'s 2000 _[Finding Forrester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finding_Forrester "Finding Forrester")_.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-39) In September 2006, Coleman released the album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_. Recorded live in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen"), Germany, in 2005, it was his first album of new material in ten years. It won the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") for music, making Coleman only the second jazz musician (after [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis")) to win the prize.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Pulitzer-40) ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Personal life")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Ornette_Coleman.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman.jpg) Coleman playing his [Selmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Selmer_Paris "Henri Selmer Paris") alto saxophone in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1994 Jazz pianist [Joanne Brackeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanne_Brackeen "Joanne Brackeen") stated in an interview with [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") that Coleman mentored her and gave her music lessons.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Lyon-41) Coleman married poet [Jayne Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Cortez "Jayne Cortez") in 1954. The couple divorced in 1964.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-42) They had one son, [Denardo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman"), born in 1956.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fox-43) Coleman died of [cardiac arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_arrest "Cardiac arrest") in Manhattan on June 11, 2015, aged 85.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) His funeral was a three-hour event with performances and speeches by several of his collaborators and contemporaries, including [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") and [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Remnick-44) ## Awards and honors \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Awards and honors")\] - [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, U.S. | | Genres | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") | | Occupations | Musician, bandleader, composer, improviser, poet | | Instrument | Piano | | Years active | 1956–2018 | | Labels | [Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_Records "Transition Records"), [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"), [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Records "Freedom Records"), [Hathut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathut_Records "Hathut Records"), [Enja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enja_Records "Enja Records"), [FMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMP/Free_Music_Production "FMP/Free Music Production") | Musical artist **Cecil Percival Taylor** (March 25, 1929–April 5, 2018)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Such-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Feather-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Seisdedos-3) was an American pianist and poet.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuch199361-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Yanow-5) Taylor was [classically trained](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classically_trained "Classically trained") and was one of the pioneers of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). His music is characterized by an energetic, physical approach, resulting in complex [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") often involving [tone clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_clusters "Tone clusters") and intricate [polyrhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythms "Polyrhythms"). His technique has been compared to [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument"). Referring to the number of keys on a standard piano, [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer") used the phrase "eighty-eight tuned drums" to describe Taylor's style.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-6) He has been referred to as " [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum") with contemporary-classical leanings".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Tatum-7) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Cecil Percival Taylor was born on March 25, 1929, in [Long Island City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_City "Long Island City"), [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-nytobit-8) and raised in [Corona, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona,_Queens "Corona, Queens").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) As an only child in a middle-class family, Taylor was encouraged by his mother, Almeda Ragland Taylor, to play music at an early age. He began playing piano at age six and went on to study at the [New York College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_College_of_Music "New York College of Music") and [New England Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory "New England Conservatory") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). At the New England Conservatory, Taylor majored in popular music arrangement. During his time there, he also became familiar with contemporary European [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"). [Bela Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók") and [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") notably influenced his music.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) In 1955, Taylor moved back to New York City from Boston. He formed a quartet with soprano saxophonist [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"), bassist [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), and drummer [Dennis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) Taylor's first recording, _[Jazz Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance "Jazz Advance")_, featured Lacy and was released in 1956.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-11) The recording is described by [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)") and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") in the _[Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "Penguin Guide to Jazz")_: "While there are still many nods to conventional [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") form in this set, it already points to the freedoms in which the pianist would later immerse himself."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-12) Taylor's quartet featuring Lacy also appeared at the 1957 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), which was made into the album _[At Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_(Cecil_Taylor_and_Gigi_Gryce_album) "At Newport (Cecil Taylor and Gigi Gryce album)")_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-13) Taylor collaborated with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") in 1958 on _[Stereo Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Drive "Stereo Drive")_, now available as _Coltrane Time_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-14) ## 1950s and early 1960s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1950s and early 1960s")\] Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Taylor's music grew more complex and moved away from existing jazz styles. Gigs were often hard to come by, and club owners found that Taylor's approach of playing long pieces tended to impede business.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-15) His 1959 [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") _[Looking Ahead!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_Ahead! "Looking Ahead!")_ showcased his innovation as a creator as compared to the jazz mainstream. Unlike others at the time, Taylor utilized virtuosic techniques and made swift stylistic shifts from phrase to phrase. These qualities, among others, still remained notable distinctions of his music for the rest of his life.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-16) Landmark recordings, such as _[Unit Structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures "Unit Structures")_ (1966), also appeared. Within the [Cecil Taylor Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_Unit "Cecil Taylor Unit") (a distinction that was often used at performances and recordings between 1962 and 2006 for a shifting group of sidemen), musicians were able to develop new forms of conversational interplay. In the early 1960s, an uncredited [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") worked with Taylor, jamming and appearing on at least one recording, _Four_, which was unreleased until appearing on the 2004 Ayler [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") _[Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Ghost:_Rare_&_Unissued_Recordings_(1962%E2%80%9370) "Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70)")_.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-17) By 1961, Taylor was working regularly with alto saxophonist [Jimmy Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Lyons_(saxophonist) "Jimmy Lyons (saxophonist)"), who would become one of his most important and consistent collaborators. Taylor, Lyons, and drummer [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray") (and later [Andrew Cyrille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cyrille "Andrew Cyrille")) formed the core personnel of the [Cecil Taylor Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_Unit "Cecil Taylor Unit"), Taylor's primary ensemble until Lyons' death in 1986. Lyons' playing, strongly influenced by jazz icon [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), retained a strong [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") sensibility and helped keep Taylor's increasingly [avant garde music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_music "Avant-garde music") tethered to the jazz tradition.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Kelsey-18) ## Late 1960s and 1970s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Late 1960s and 1970s")\] Taylor began to perform solo concerts in the latter half of the 1960s. The first known recorded solo performance was "Carmen With Rings" (59 minutes) in [De Doelen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Doelen "De Doelen") concert hall in [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") on July 1, 1967. Two days earlier, Taylor had played the same composition in the [Amsterdam Concertgebouw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Concertgebouw "Amsterdam Concertgebouw"). Many of his later concerts were released on album and include _[Indent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indent_(album) "Indent (album)")_ (1973), side one of _[Spring of Two Blue-J's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_of_Two_Blue_J's "Spring of Two Blue J's")_ (1973), _[Silent Tongues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_Tongues "Silent Tongues")_ (1974), _[Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_(album) "Garden (album)")_ (1982), _[For Olim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Olim "For Olim")_ (1987), _[Erzulie Maketh Scent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erzulie_Maketh_Scent "Erzulie Maketh Scent")_ (1989), and _[The Tree of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tree_of_Life_(Cecil_Taylor_album) "The Tree of Life (Cecil Taylor album)")_ (1998).[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-19) He began to garner critical and popular acclaim, playing for [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") on the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") Lawn,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-20) lecturing as an [artist-in-residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist-in-residence "Artist-in-residence") at universities, and eventually being awarded a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") in 1973.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-21) In 1976, Taylor directed a production of [Adrienne Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Kennedy "Adrienne Kennedy")'s _[A Rat's Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Rat's_Mass "A Rat's Mass")_ at [La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_MaMa_Experimental_Theatre_Club "La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club") in the [East Village of Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Village,_Manhattan "East Village, Manhattan"). His production combined the original script with a chorus of orchestrated voices used as instruments. [Jimmy Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Lyons_(saxophonist) "Jimmy Lyons (saxophonist)"), [Rashid Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashid_Bakr_(musician) "Rashid Bakr (musician)"), [Andy Bey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Bey "Andy Bey"), [Karen Borca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Borca "Karen Borca"), [David S. Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_S._Ware "David S. Ware") and [Raphe Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphe_Malik "Raphe Malik") performed in the production as the Cecil Taylor Unit, among other musicians and actors.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-22) ## 1980s, 1990s, and the Feel Trio \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1980s, 1990s, and the Feel Trio")\] Following Lyons' death in 1986, Taylor formed the Feel Trio in the late 1980s with [William Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Parker_(musician) "William Parker (musician)") on bass and [Tony Oxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Oxley "Tony Oxley") on drums. The group can be heard on _[Celebrated Blazons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrated_Blazons "Celebrated Blazons")_, _[Looking (Berlin Version) The Feel Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_(Berlin_Version)_The_Feel_Trio "Looking (Berlin Version) The Feel Trio")_ and the 10-disc set _[2 Ts for a Lovely T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_Ts_for_a_Lovely_T "2 Ts for a Lovely T")_.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-25) Compared to his prior groups with Lyons, the Feel Trio had a more abstract approach, tethered less to jazz tradition and more aligned with the ethos of European [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation"). He also performed with larger ensembles and [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") projects. Taylor's extended residence in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") in 1988 was documented by the German label [FMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMP_(Free_Music_Production) "FMP (Free Music Production)"), resulting in a [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") of performances in duet and trio with a large number of European free improvisors, including Oxley, [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Han Bennink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Bennink "Han Bennink"), [Tristan Honsinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_Honsinger "Tristan Honsinger"), [Louis Moholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Moholo "Louis Moholo"), and [Paul Lovens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lovens "Paul Lovens"). Most of his later recordings have been released on European labels, with the exception of _[Momentum Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_Space_(album) "Momentum Space (album)")_ (a meeting with [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") and [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones")) on [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records")/Gitanes. The classical label [Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_Records "Bridge Records") released his 1998 [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") performance _Algonquin_, a duet with violinist [Mat Maneri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat_Maneri "Mat Maneri").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-26) Taylor continued to perform for capacity audiences around the world with live concerts, usually playing his favored instrument, a [Bösendorfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6sendorfer "Bösendorfer") piano featuring nine extra lower-register keys. In 1987, he toured England with Australian pianist [Roger Woodward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Woodward "Roger Woodward"), presenting recitals on which Woodward played solo works by [Xenakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iannis_Xenakis "Iannis Xenakis"), [Takemitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toru_Takemitsu "Toru Takemitsu"), and [Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Feldman "Morton Feldman"), followed by Taylor, also playing solo.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-27) A [documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film") on Taylor, entitled [_All the Notes_](https://web.archive.org/web/20080924143425/http://www.chrisfelver.com/films/taylor.html), was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") in 2006 by director [Chris Felver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Felver "Chris Felver"). Taylor was also featured in a 1981 documentary film entitled _[Imagine the Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_the_Sound "Imagine the Sound")_, in which he discusses and performs his music, poetry, and dance.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-28) In 1993, he was awarded a [MacArthur Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows_Program "MacArthur Fellows Program").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-30) ## 2000s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 2000s")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg/250px-Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg) Cecil Taylor, Buffalo, New York Taylor recorded sparingly in the 2000s, but continued to perform with his own ensembles (the Cecil Taylor Ensemble and the Cecil Taylor Big Band) and with other musicians such as [Joe Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Locke_(musician) "Joe Locke (musician)"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), and [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-31) In 2004, the Cecil Taylor Big Band at the [Iridium Jazz Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iridium_Jazz_Club "Iridium Jazz Club") was nominated a best performance of 2004 by [All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-AAJ-32) The Cecil Taylor Trio was nominated for the same at the [Highline Ballroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highline_Ballroom "Highline Ballroom") in 2009.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-AAJ09-33) The trio consisted of Taylor, Albey Balgochian, and [Jackson Krall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Krall "Jackson Krall"). In 2010, Triple Point Records released a deluxe [limited-edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited-edition "Limited-edition") double [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") titled _[Ailanthus/Altissima: Bilateral Dimensions of 2 Root Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ailanthus/Altissima:_Bilateral_Dimensions_of_2_Root_Songs "Ailanthus/Altissima: Bilateral Dimensions of 2 Root Songs")_, a set of duos with Taylor's longtime collaborator [Tony Oxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Oxley "Tony Oxley") that was recorded live at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-34) In 2013, he was awarded the [Kyoto Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Prize_in_Arts_and_Philosophy "Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy") for Music.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Guardian_obit-35) He was described as "An Innovative Jazz Musician Who Has Fully Explored the Possibilities of Piano Improvisation".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Kyoto-36) In 2014, his career and 85th birthday were honored at the [Painted Bride Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painted_Bride_Art_Center "Painted Bride Art Center") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") with the tribute concert event "Celebrating Cecil".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-37) In 2016, Taylor received a retrospective at the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art") entitled "Open Plan: Cecil Taylor".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-38) In 2008, Taylor performed with [Pauline Oliveros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Oliveros "Pauline Oliveros") at the [Curtis R Priem Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Media_and_Performing_Arts_Center "Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center") at [Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rensselaer_Polytechnic_Institute "Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute"). The concert was recorded and is available on a DVD which also features a 75-minute video of a Taylor poetry recital entitled _Floating Gardens: The Poetry Of Cecil Taylor_.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-40) Taylor, along with dancer [Min Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min_Tanaka "Min Tanaka"), was the subject of [Amiel Courtin-Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiel_Courtin-Wilson "Amiel Courtin-Wilson")'s 2016 documentary film _The Silent Eye_.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-41) ## Ballet and dance \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Ballet and dance")\] In addition to piano, Taylor was always interested in ballet and dance. His mother, who died while he was young, was a dancer and played the piano and violin. Taylor once said: "I try to imitate on the piano the leaps in space a dancer makes."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-42) He collaborated with dancer [Dianne McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_McIntyre "Dianne McIntyre") from the mid 1970s to the early 1980s.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-43) In 1979, he composed and played the music for a 12-minute ballet, "Tetra Stomp: Eatin' Rain in Space", featuring [Mikhail Baryshnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Baryshnikov "Mikhail Baryshnikov") and [Heather Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heather_Watts "Heather Watts").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-44) ## Poetry \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Poetry")\] Taylor was a poet, and cited [Robert Duncan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Duncan_(poet) "Robert Duncan (poet)"), [Charles Olson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Olson "Charles Olson"), and [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka") as major influences.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-45) He often integrated his poems into his musical performances, and they frequently appear in the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") of his albums. The album _[Chinampas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinampas_(album) "Chinampas (album)")_, released by [Leo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Records "Leo Records") in 1987, is a recording of Taylor reciting several of his poems while accompanying himself on percussion.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-46) His poetry was likened to his music primarily by the ways in which Taylor alters and transforms material both linguistic and musical.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-47) ## Musical style and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Musical style and legacy")\] According to Steven Block, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") originated with Taylor's performances at the [Five Spot Cafe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in 1957 and with [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") in 1959.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-48) In 1964, Taylor co-founded the [Jazz Composers Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Composers_Guild "Jazz Composers Guild") to enhance opportunities for [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") musicians.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Walden-49) Taylor's style and methods have been described as " [constructivist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructivism_(art) "Constructivism (art)")".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-50) Despite [Scott Yanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Yanow "Scott Yanow")'s warning regarding Taylor's "forbidding music" ("Suffice it to say that Cecil Taylor's music is not for everyone"), he praises Taylor's "remarkable technique and endurance", and his "advanced", "radical", "original", and uncompromising "musical vision".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Yanow-5) This musical vision is a large part of Taylor's legacy: > Playing with Taylor I began to be liberated from thinking about chords. I'd been imitating John Coltrane unsuccessfully and because of that I was really chord conscious. — [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), quoted in [LeRoi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka"), album liner notes for _Four for Trane_ (Impulse A-71, 1964) Scott Yanow of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") wrote: "Taylor's high-energy atonalism fit in well with the free jazz of the period but he was actually leading the way rather than being part of a movement. \[...\] In fact, it could be safely argued that no jazz music of the era approached the ferocity and intensity of Cecil Taylor's."[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-51) ## Personal life and death \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Personal life and death")\] Taylor moved to [Fort Greene, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Greene,_Brooklyn "Fort Greene, Brooklyn"), in 1983.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) He died at his Brooklyn residence on April 5, 2018, at the age of 89.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-53) At the time of his death, Taylor was working on an autobiography and future concerts, among other projects.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Cecil_Taylor_Website-54) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [Cecil Taylor discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_discography "Cecil Taylor discography") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: References")\] 01. See Wikipedia's [guide to writing better articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") for suggestions._(October 2023)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | The term " **M-Base**" is a term coined in the 1980s by American musician [Steve Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coleman "Steve Coleman") to describe a new theory about creative expression. "M-Base-concept" is short for " **m** acro **-b** asic **a** rray of **s** tructured **e** xtemporization", and critics have used this term to categorize this scene's music as a style of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-1) But Coleman stressed "M-Base" doesn't denote a musical style but a way of thinking about creating music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-2) However, Coleman has expressed discomfort with the term “jazz” to describe his music and also says M-Base was intended to be more expansive than describing music alone. M-Base was associated with a loose collective of young African American musicians and other performers active in and around [Brooklyn, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn,_New_York "Brooklyn, New York"). The M-Base collective included Coleman, [Graham Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Haynes "Graham Haynes"), [Cassandra Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_Wilson "Cassandra Wilson"), [Geri Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_Allen "Geri Allen"), [Robin Eubanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Eubanks "Robin Eubanks"), and [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby"). However, the musicians of the M-Base movement, which also included dancers and poets, strived for common creative musical languages, so their early recordings show many similarities reflecting their common ideas, the experiences of working together, and their similar cultural background. To label this kind of music, jazz critics have established the word "M-Base" as a jazz style for lack of a better term, distorting its original meaning.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-3) ## Music associated with the term "M-Base" \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music associated with the term \"M-Base\"")\] In 1991 a significant number of M-Base participants labelled as "M-Base Collective" recorded the CD _Anatomy of a Groove_. Most of them previously contributed to CDs by alto saxophonist Steve Coleman, whose creativity has been a pivotal factor in that movement,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-4) although he refused to be called its leader or founder. Coleman and his friend Greg Osby, who plays alto saxophone in a related style, together led the group Strata Institute, which recorded two CDs (the second with tenor saxophonist Von Freeman as a further leader). Under the name of Osby, a number of CDs with a specific character have been released starting in 1987, which also coined the perception of "M-Base" jazz. Tenor saxophonist and flutist Gary Thomas admittedly didn't take part in the M-Base initiative, but joined them, and there were similarities in his way of playing. He can be heard on recordings of Coleman and Osby, and his own CDs are also labelled as "M-Base-style". All three saxophonists contributed to the CD _[Jumpworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumpworld "Jumpworld")_ by singer Cassandra Wilson. Pianist [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)") said about Greg Osby: "He has an incredible sense of rhythm and harmonic accuracy, and picks the right notes with a precision that isn't common to people with his technical versatility. He's developed into a fully rounded artist who can play various styles extremely well – better than most."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-5) Greg Osby said about [Gary Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Thomas_(musician) "Gary Thomas (musician)"): "He's extremely intelligent and has a capacity for absorption that exceeds that of most people that I know \[…\] He has his own compositional and improvisational method that is peerless in my opinion. He's my favourite tenor saxophone player on the contemporary scene."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-6) Clarinettist and composer Don Byron called Steve Coleman "an exceptional personality of American music history."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-7) Antecedents to M-Base were identified by jazz critic [Bill Milkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Milkowski "Bill Milkowski") as the [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")-led band featured on recordings like 1975's _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_; he noted the combination of [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune")'s acerbic saxophone lines atop the syncopated [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)") performed by the rhythm section of drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), and rhythm guitarist [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-8) ## Further history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Further history")\] The ideas of the M-Base concept were largely incompatible with the requirements of music business. Most participants of the M-Base movement turned to more conventional music. Cassandra Wilson's blues- and folk-influenced music has been fairly suitable for an adaption to the taste of a larger audience. Wilson has been signed to [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") since 1993. Though two of Gary Thomas' recordings were highly rated by _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-9) he only had a contract with a small European company and his performance opportunities were virtually limited to Europe. Since 1997, he has put his career as a bandleader on hold to teach at Peabody Music Institute.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-10) Greg Osby signed with Blue Note Records in 1990 and developed a specific balancing act between an enhanced reverence to tradition and maintaining his new direction. In 2008, Osby launched his own small label.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-11) Steve Coleman has developed his music further in accordance with the M-Base concept. In the 1990s his CDs were released by the major label [BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Music_Group "Bertelsmann Music Group"). Thereafter he became practically an underground artist in the U.S. again, in that his music was only available as imports, distributed by a small French label.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-12) In 2007 [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn")'s small label [Tzadik Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzadik_Records "Tzadik Records") released a solo CD of Coleman. In 2010 the small advanced label [Pi Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi_Recordings "Pi Recordings") began to release Steve Coleman's recordings. Although the musical line initially called "M-Base" became more than ever focused on Steve Coleman, a number of younger musicians (e.g. a range of excellent drummers) have made substantial creative contributions to his music and his influence is to be found in several musical fields – both in terms of music technique and of the music's meaning. Pianist [Vijay Iyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Iyer "Vijay Iyer") (who was chosen as "Jazz Musician of the Year 2010" by the [Jazz Journalists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Journalists_Association "Jazz Journalists Association")) said, "It's hard to overstate Steve \[Coleman's\] influence. He's affected more than one generation, as much as anyone since John Coltrane. It's not just that you can connect the dots by playing seven or 11 beats. What sits behind his influence is this global perspective on music and life. He has a point of view of what he does and why he does it."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-13) ## M-Base concept \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: M-Base concept")\] Steve Coleman explained the substantial elements of the concept as: - improvisation and structure - contemporary relevance - music as expression of life experience - growth through creativity and philosophical broadening - use of non-western concepts The M-Base concept reminds of the creative energy of the bebop originators, their loose collective, and also of their musical goals.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-14) The concept does not include "neo-classical jazz", [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") music without structures, [fusion music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_music "Fusion music"), music which isn't mainly improvised, or music shaped with respect to commercial aspects. ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: References")\] 01.
